I call the attention of the government to a telegraphic despatch in this morning's paper in reference to an article in the London 'Standard' which states that negotiations towards a treaty are going on between the Canadian government and Germany. I ask the Prime Minister if there have been at any time such negotiations, and if they are proceeding at present.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There are not nor have there been any such negotiations as those referred to. From time to time we have had opportunities of meeting gentlemen interested in German trade who have discussed with us the advisability of certain changes, but there are no negotiations; nothing which would correspond to the statement made in the press.
Is it the intention of the Minister of Finance to go on with his budget speech next Thursday ?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My present expectation is to bring the budget on Thursday. If anything intervenes to change that intention it will be announced to-morrow.

Is it possible for the Minister of Finance to give any information as to whether the government contemplates any changes in the customs duties? I specially refer to the duties on tin. This is a time of activity in that particular business; the farmers and the canning establishments are providing themselves with supplies, and as I have received many inquiries I bring the matter to the attention of the Minister of Finance.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If my hon. friend reflects for a moment, he will see from his own experience that it is never possible for a Finance Minister to make any statement as to the intention of the government in tariff matters except in the budget speech, and I shall have to ask my hon. friend to be patient until that is delivered.
I merely wished to ask the Minister of Finance if he could state that there would be no change in the tariff.
The Finance Minister, having become a protectionist, will surely see that the tin plate industry is protected.

Mr. Speaker, I quite appreciate what the Minister of Finance has said, that he has locked up securely in his own mind the knowledge of the great benefits he is about to confer on Canada by the budget which he will bring down on Thursday next, and it is in order that we may improve, if possible, the text of the deliverance which he shall then make, and if possible bring about an improvement of conditions, that I propose to invite the attention of the Finance Minister for a few moments to the condition of the woollen industry of Canada at the present time. The importance of that industry very few, I think, will be disposed to question. There may or may not be some who feel some doubt as to the extent to which we can develop that industry. Speaking for myself, I am convinced that with proper governmental regulations there is in Canada a field for an enormous development of the woollen industry both as regards production and manufacture. As a farmer, of course my attention will be directed more particularly to the matter from the point of view of the farming industry; but I shall not forget that for an all-round industry we require not only the production but also the manufacture of wool. A business government, I presume, will keep in mind especially the main industry of the country. A wise business man, while giving regard to all details, will endeavour especially to conserve that which is his main source of income. Therefore I

think I am right in saying that above all other interests the interest of farming in Canada should be the main concern of a wise and prudent adminstration.
In the early days of the session, in answer to questions I asked, the government informed me that in 1908 we had
575.000	farmers; that there were maintained and supported directly by farming
3.788.000	people, considerably more than one-half of our entire population; that there was invested in farming in Canada $1,761,486,180; that the field crops of last year were of the value of $432,000,000; and that our export of grains, animals, and other farm products, amounted to $129,000,000, after supplying all our own home wants. Now, the greatest industry of the greatest nations of the world is that of textiles, among them being France, Germany, Belgium, Holland, Great Britain, and the United States, and it ought to be of concern to us to consider very carefully whether we can develope in Canada a great textile industry, and particularily that branch of it known as the woollen industry.
Great Britain, with a population of 44,000,000, has 5,000,000, or more than one-ninth of its entire population, engaged in the textile industry; and it is surely a moderate computation to say that in addition to supporting themselves, each of these will on the average support two others. If so, we have the result that in Great Britain the textile industry gives employment to more than one-ninth and gives support directly to more than one-third of the entire population of the country. In acreage, Great Britain is of course a comparatively small country; yet it has developed an enormous woollen industry, both as regards the production of wool and the manufacture of woollens. In 1907 the woollen manufactures of Great Britain amounted to $464,000,000, of which $185,000,000 worth was for export and $278,000,000 worth for home consumption. Let me interject here that important as is the export, it is even more vitally important that every country should be in a position to clothe itself, so far as the staples of clothing for its people are concerned. Britain, within its narrow boundaries, produces 131,000,000 pounds of wool annually, while we, with our almost illimitable territory, produce 12,000,000 pounds annually. Britain within its narrow confines,is able to support 30,000,000 sheep, while we in Canada, with our vast extent of country, can only support about 2,000,000 sheep, although in 1905, showing to what extent this industry has declined, Ontario alone had more than 2,000,000 sheep. Canada is at present importing upwards of $22,000,000 worth of woollen fabrics to clothe
Mi-. LENNOX.
its _ people, almost every dollar's worth of which should be produced and manufactured in our own country, if we had a tariff suitable to the conditions of Canada.
France has directly engaged in the textile industry 2,008;000 people, supporting a population of 6,000,000 or 7,000,000 people, equal or more than equal to the entire population of the Dominion of Canada. Germany, as we know, protects everything, and it has engaged in the textile industry almost two to every one engaged in any other industry.
Coming to the United States, we come to a country similar in almost all respects to our own. The history of the United States should be our history practically, as regards the woollen industry. I know that there are some divergencies, but they are of such minor character that what the United States has done in the century that was hers, Canada in this century, which the Prime Minister says is our century, ought to do in the woollen industry for the people of Canada. The conditions in our maritime provinces and in our western provinces of British Columbia, Alberta and Saskatchewan are just as favourable to the production of wool as are those in the United States. In fact, a large and important element in the manufacture of woollens in the United States is derived from Canada. Among the best worsteds produced in the United States are those manufactured from Canadian wool. In fact the conditions in the United States are identical with those in Canada plus the protection they give their farmers on their native wool. That is about the difference reduced to actual analysis. It takes time for nations to realize what is in their interest. This government has had twelve years' time in which to realize it, and so far have failed to do so. It took time in the United States. There was a period when the United States was sacrificing its interests in favour of British wool manufacturing. As late as 1799 the United States was taking 40 per cent of the entire woollen export of Britain. As late as 1816-although the war of 1812 had checked the inroads and had made the United States, for the time being, realize the importance of being commercially independent of any other nation for its clothing- the United States were importing as much as an average of $70,000,000 a year from Britain. But the war of 1812 drew attention to the fact that it was necessary for the United States to do something. In the years preceding the war, in 1808, for instance, the United States was only producing a matter of 14,000,000 pounds of wool, but by the time the war was closing, it was producing 22,000,000 pounds. Now that country is producing 330,000,000 pounds and is manufacturing into woollens 500,000,000 pounds, so that the United States to-day, with conditions similar to our own,is actually producing upon its own farms two-thirds of

the entire wool which it manufactures into clothing. What are we going to do? The question is an important one, and the history of the United States is pregnant with information to show us what we ought to be able to do. I might say that in 1812, before the United States had taken reasonable measures to protect its trade in that respect, prices had, by reason of the war increased to an enormous extent. As a matter of fact broad cloth sold in that country at from $8 to $12 a yard, and merino rams sold as high as $1,000 each. After the war scare was over, the United States became careless again, and Britain again obtained a foothold there, with the effect that sheep sold as low as $1 a head, and they were importing from Britain to the enormous extent of $70,000,000 of woollen manufactures.
From the history of the United States, I shall proceed to refer, in a moment or two to the history of Britain in this matter; but I deduce this proposition, which I submit for the consideration of the government, that a really successful national woollen industry in Canada involves a profitable production of wool as well as profitable manufacture of woollens, and it should be the aim of the government to harmonize, unite and merge these two great interests. Speaking from a farmer's standpoint more particularly, I am convinced that the first essential is the production of wool. The production of wool is a native industry of Canada. It prospered in the early settlement of Canada before tariffs began to interfere with it: and Tory as I am-if you call me such-I am yet prepared to say that as yet, neither Conservatives nor Liberals- the latter used to call themselves reformers when I was young, but reformers have gone out of business-have done all they could for the basis of the woollen industry in Canada, which is of course the production of our native wool.
We have been protecting the manufacturers, and it is important that we should do so. They are the great source of profit from the raw material, the production of which cannot reach its climax of profit until it is manufactured into woollens in this country. Therefore I do not ignore the great importance of protecting the woollen industry, but I would point out that both parties have been beginning at the wrong end. They should begin at the foundation and not at the upper story. They should begin by encouraging the growth of wool, which is the basis of a healthy, substantial, progressive woollen industry in Canada. We have no end of millions for industrial enterprises in this country. We have millions for iron and steel bounties, but we have not yet had a square deal for the farmers with regard to their woollen industry.
What did Britain do in this matter- free trade Britain, "whose example our hon.
friends opposite are so prone to praise but not to follow? Free trade Britain was the victim of other countries for a time. She took a long time to wake up. Six or seven hundred years ago she was paying tribute to the continent in the woollen industry. At that time Britain, which now stands supreme in the woollen trade, was hardly in the running at all, and Belgium and Holland were then leading the trade of the world in that respect. They were spoken of as clothing the world and they were making clothing to a large extent out of woollens manufactured from the fleeces produced in Britain; so that those countries were reaping a rich reward while the British were practically the hewers of wood and drawers of water or rather the clippers of wool for the continent. To such an extent was this the case that the expression 'rich as a Count of Flanders,' was generally used to describe the flourishing condition of those who were deriving large profits from raw material exported from Britain to be manufactured into woollen goods on the continent. Well, I have no objection that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, who is practically the King of Canada at present, should follow the example set him by some of the Kings of Britain and do something in this matter.

and King Edward I. tried to do something in this matter. But it was to King Edward III. that we owe the establishment of that great industry in Britain, the textile industry. He saw that Great Britain could never be supreme-and it never would have been supreme, either commercially, navally or nationally-if it continued under the system that prevailed in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, the system of exporting its fleeces for manufacture abroad, and buying back the goods at enhanced prices to clothe its people later on. So, King Edward III. took measures, and most effective measures. He first encouraged Flemish wool growers to come in considerable numbers and establish themselves in Great Britain. He then 'sent emissaries to the continent and placed such inducements before the people there as led large numbers of Flemish artisans and wool-workers to come and settle in Great Britain. All this was not accomplished without much negotiation and deplomacy or without marked hostility on the part of some sections of the people of Great Britain; as members of the House will recollect, thousands of these Flemish artisans were driven out by the hostile artisans and labourers of Great Britain. But the King persisted, and the government persisted too. And they went farther; they enacted a law which stands, perhaps at the very base of all the prosperity of Great Britain in connection with textiles, and which is probably the

most drastic piece of protective legislation that has ever been enacted in any country. This was enacted in free-trade Britain in the reign of King Edward III. It provided that no Welshman, Irishman or Englishman-I do not know why it specifies the classes, but I give it as it is in the statute-should export wool or fleeces from Great Britain under penalty of death. And so the textile industry of Great Britain had its foundation and its growth. Statute succeeded statute, down through the various reigns, prohibiting the export of textile machinery, protecting and guarding the secrets in connection with the woollen industry and otherwise giving to the industry the assistance of the law. This continued down through the centuries until the reign of Queen Victoria and to the year 1854. And so it was only by centuries of protection of the most drastic. character that Great Britain was able to build up its textile industry until it felt that for a time- and that time is now nearly exhausted- it could defy all trade competitors wherever they .might be. And thus we see that the textile industry of Great Britain, like that of the United States, was fostered and built up by means of trade and tariff laws. It is clear that the conditions of Canada and the United States at least are so similar that what was done in the United States we can do in Canada by proper adjustment of our statutes. If that be so, then it becomes merely a question of what aTe the government going to do in this matter for the interests of Canada? There are a number of practical men here in the House, and these men know that one of the great ultimate profits in manufacturing to-day is through the utilization of the by-products. This may not be the largest profit in a manufacturing business, but it is in a sense the unexpected one, almost the unearned one, and it is one of the most important in connection with any manufacture. It is important that we should grow wool in Canada even if we do not manufacture it. It is important that we should grow wheat in Canada, although a large portion of it is exported in the form of wheat instead of being first converted into flora. It is important that we should bring the logs from the forest, even if we export them in that form. But it is far better, as everybody knows, if we can carry the process further and export the finished product in every case. The great national by-product of the raw materials of Canada is secured by the manufacture in Canada, as far as possible, of the raw materials into the finished article. In this way we shall increase the population and multiply demand. There will be more to be housed, more to be fed, more to be clothed, more to be carried, more to be lighted, more to be provided for in every way. In this way, you will secure that result which Conservatives have been trying to point out to Liberals for so Mr. LENNOX.
long, which we tried to impress upon them for eighteen years while they were in opposition - that by this means we can enormously benefit the country nationally through extending and increasing the home market and benefiting our entire population. It would be as wise for us to export our wheat and import it back in the form of flour, paying for the carriage and paying for the foreign manufacture, as to export our wool and buy it back in the form of clothing, whether made up or otherwise. We cannot build up a great woollen industry so long as we export our fleeces and buy them back as manufactured goods. We must form a full partnership union-to borrow a phrase from an hon. member of this House-between these two great interests; we must not only raise wool, but we must spin it and weave it and wear it, if we are to develop a great and prosperous, all-round woollen industry in Canada.
If we survey our situation in Canada we have every reason to believe that we can develop a great woollen industry in this country. I would call the attention of the Minister of Finance to the fact that we have in Canada immense areas which are especially adapted to the growth and production of wool, but which are, perhaps, not adapted for any other profitable use. I have endeavoured to ascertain the extent of land of that character in Canada, but I have not been able to secure any very definite information upon that point. However, every one who takes any note of the conditions in the country is aware that we have immense areas of the kind I have described. Another important feature in favour of wool-growing in Canada is the peculiar immunity from disease of Canadian sheep. It is an absolute, well-established fact that perhaps in no other country in the world are sheep as free from disease as they are in Canada. As a matter of fact, it has been ascertained, and this information will be found in a publication ol the Department of Agriculture, that herds imported into Canada and which had suffered from disease in other countries for generations have, after two or three generations in Canada, become entirely free of disease. Then, too, the exceedingly high quality of the mutton produced in Canada is an important factor. I admit that it is not equal in texture or in flavour to the English mutton, but it is equal to any other mutton in the world. To-day it is greatly sought after by people in the United States, hotel-keepers and others who -want a high class article. That is notably the case in the maritime provinces where every fall purchasers for American hotels buy large quantities of mutton. Although there has been some doubt as to the quality of our wool, it is well established that we can grow not only

the coarser, but also the finer grades, particularly since the west is opening up and we are now producing an excellent quality of wool which is being used in the United States. I do not know whether the Canadian woollen manufacturers are doing all in their power to assist the Canadian producer by using his wool. Then we have the important factor to which I have already referred, that our conditions are similar to those in the United States where they have developed an enormous woollen industry.
The last, and perhaps the most important fact, is that Canada contains, in a sense, the last great fields, the last sheep walks of the world. We know that as agriculture becomes more settled, the sheep walks are more circumscribed. That is the case in Australia and in the United States, and notably in England and on the continent of Europe; but for years, and I venture to say for scores and for hundreds of years, as we spread out and carry our railways further into the interior and the remote regions of Canada, more and more, we will open up valuable fields where we can produce wool with great profit to the people. I venture to predict that a business government,^ whenever it comes into power in Ottawa, if this government will not rise to the occasion, will so encourage and develop the woollen industry that it will become a great factor in planting on this northern half of the continent one of the greatest nations in the world.
Woollen manufacturing has succeeded in the United States and it succeeded here as long as the wool farmer and the manufacturer worked in harmony. It was a native industry with the French colonists in Quebec and Nova Scotia years ago, and with the English colonists in Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick and Ontario; they were successfully producing their own wool and manufacturing it into clothing. The industry prospered until thirty years ago, when the laws of Canada virtually divorced the interests of the farmers and the manuacturers. Now we are losing ground; I do not think there can be much doubt about that. It could hardly be otherwise. No attention is paid to this industry, the government knows it, they know ^ they have been jollying the farmer and jollying the manufacturer. There is perhaps no greater instance of that than the speech of the right hon. gentleman at the manufacturers' convention at Montreal. But they have been doing absolutely nothing, and year after year these great industries of wool growing and wool manufacturing have been losing ground. The farmer has been keeping fewer sheep, producing less wool and receiving less money for it; he has been going out of the business because there has been no profit in it. The
manufacturers, year after year, have been going behind; factory after factory has been closing up and selling its machinery, as this Montreal factory is now .selling its machinery and returning it to Great Britain. It could hardly be otherwise, because when I asked the Minister of Customs the other day for statistics in reference to the woollen industry the minister, always accommodating, always kind, had to confess to me that he had no information; that there were no statistics and nothing available.
I find in a copy of the Yorkshire 'Post' of February 24 last, which was sent to me, a dispatch from Ottawa of the 11th of February, reporting a meeting of the Dominion Sheep Breeders' Association. These gentlemen have been gauging the situation and have come to the conclusion that this government are doing nothing and do not appear to be awake to the situation at all. The report reads:
The Dominion Sheep Breeders' Association, acting on this advice, appointed a committee in January to wait upon the Minister of Customs to present the case for the protection of raw wool. At the annual meeting of the association, held in Toronto last Friday, this committee, whose chairman was Mr. John Campbell, president of the association, presented its report, which was read by its secretary, Col. D. A. McCrae. The committee, said Colonel McCrae, had been sympathetically received by Mr. Paterson, Minister of Customs, but found that both Mr. Paterson and his staff were lamentably unfamiliar with the actual situation of the wool trade
In Mr. Paterson's opinion, little could be done to remedy the situation

Very much like the fly on the wheel policy of some years ago.
-In: informed the committee, unless special legislation were enacted by the Dominion parliament

Why don't you get a hustle on and enact the legislation if it is necessary? Why don't you do something for the sheep breeders of -Canada? That is what I am after. We have not yet had the budget speech, and I have a kind of faith that even at the last hour the Minister of Finance may repent and see the wisdom of doing something for the wool grower and the woollen manufacturer of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is it that my hon. friend asks to be done?
Oh well now, that is all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I knew that was al1 right.
That is all right. I did not want to move a vote of want of confidence in this government to day, but I may say that as far as my heart goes I could do it all right.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Hear, hear; nobody doubts that.

It would be perfectly right, but in the end I am going to summarize what I think the government ought to do. If this government do not know what ought to be done after all the interviews they have had with woollen manufacturers and sheep breeders' associations and representatives of the woollen industries generally in Canada it is time that they would leave and I think it is time now. I think there is good ground for believing that as these gentlemen, whilst they were out of power, failed to appreciate the conditions which would bring prosperity to Canada, so now they are not able, as regards the woollen industry, to appreciate the situation. Let me illustrate the matter, By quoting the following figures with reference to the sheep industry in Ontario, which is the only province for which we have statistics;

In all Canada to-day we have about two million sheep less than we had in Ontario in 1895. We have had a shrinkage, since 1895, of 45 per cent in the number of sheep kept in Ontario, while in other lines agriculture is profitable. It is prospering in spite of the action of my hon. friends opposite, as the following figures will show:

Increase 58 per cent. We are losing ground in the sheep raising industry and we are losing ground notably and dreadfully m the matter of our manufacturing facilities. In 1899 we had in Canada 270 woollen mills in pretty steady operation, I believe. Now he have 190. We have lost 80 or 30 per cent of the lot. There has been a shrinkage of 30 per cent in the number of woollen mills in Canada, and a shrinkage in output of, I venture to say, at least 50 per cent.
My hon. friend the Finance Minister asked me what we would propose. Well, we are prepared to take upon ourselves the burden of doing what is in the best interests of Canada at any time, but Mr. LENNOX.
I would propose that the government should do something that would prevent this industry, as far as the farm is concerned, from languishing from year to year. It is a necessary adjunct to the farm, and I would commend to the hon. gentleman a sentence from a pamphlet on wool and woollens which I dare say the Minister of Finance has read, and which I regard as a very careful and clever statement upon the subject. It is by Mr. E. B. Biggar. I quote as follows:
The foundation of the woollen industry is wool, and the protection that Canada needs to re-establish this industry is a system that will begin with the sheep-raiser and continue by progressive stages to the spinner, the weaver and the knitter, and on to the clothing manufacturer.
I will read another sentence from the ' Yorkshire Post ', and this is in connection with the position that the Dominion Sheep Breeder's Association take upon the question. The paper says:
The argument of the advocates of duties on wool was, that if, along with duties on raw wool, the manufacturers were protected by compensatory duties, then there would spring up all over Canada a great many factories for the manufacture of worsteds, for which purpose the wools grown in Canada were especially valuable. They were at present being shipped into the United States, and were used there for the manufacture of what were described as ' the best clothes in the world.' There was no reason why the wool growers and the wool manufacturers should not be able to work in harmony to bring about a revival of what ought to be one of the greatest industries of the country. It was therefore resolved that the committee which had been appointed to interview the authorities at Ottawa should appoint a sub-oommittee to meet the representatives of the wool manufacturers and discuss the situation together.
As to what would happen as the result of our protecting ourselves, protecting the farmers and the industries of Canada, I want to read a line or two quoted from an interview in the ' Dewsbury District News ' of September 26, 1908, with a Batleyite manufacturere, a very prominent manufacturer in England. He says:
The near approach of the general election in Canada gives rise to a good deal of anxiety in their country. It is well known here that Canadian manufacturers are suffering most acutely from British competition.
That is the position as they view it in England. Then, after some other questions he is asked:
' Would it not be worth your while to establish mills in Canada? ' ' Most decidedly ' was the ready answer. ' We have spent a lot of money in recent years on new machinery. If we had put that plant down in Canada we could have made big profits, assisted by the present tariff, and if the tariff wall is raised so high that our goods are shut out, you will

see new mills opened in Canada by English firms, who will beat the Canadians on their own grounds/

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I say ' hear, hear ' with all gusto in response to my hon. friend. In other words if you protect our people, instead of protecting the people of Britain and other countries-and charity in this respect begins at home-you will have with respect to this industry what happened with reference to kindred industries in the United States, when 130 branch industries of the United States-such as the Deering Harvester concern-established their works in Canada. This Batleyite manufacturer says that if we had been ready to protect ourselves, or if in the workings of Providence the Conservatives had come into power and had asserted what is in the interest of the people of Canada, the English manufacturers would have established their mills in Canada. He says:
The Canadian manufacturers must not think that protection will save them. If they cannot make cloth at the price at which it ought to be made they will be driven out of the business by stress of competition, even if we are compelled to build factories in Canada to enable us to do it.
My own firm is prepared to open a mill there next year if such step is necessary to protect our interests in that country and to offer inducements to our employees to go there.
The right hon. gentleman must realize, the Minister of Finance must realize that you have only to adopt the square deal towards the people of Canada, and instead of having foreign goods, or even goods from Britain coming in and closing up our factories, you will have healthy competition in Canada, no increase in price, and you will have a large number of factories from England and elsewhere establishing branches and building up an immense woollen trade here. Then he touches a crucial point, and I commend this to my right hon. friend; he says:
The worst of it is that high protection tariffs drive industry out of our own country and that means loss to each of our local authorities through reduced revenues for gas, electricity, and in rates, and loss to the shopkeepers.
High protective tariffs in Canada entail loss on the foreign country, and on Britain, and the result is, as he says, that they have to transfer their industries into the protected country, and so the municipal revenues are transferred to the protected country. That is an item worth considering. So it is that if you will give reasonable and adequate protection to the industries of Canada you will be securing for Canada that great national by-product that results from the manufacture of the raw material 131
into the completed article within our own country. I am not an expert in the woollen industry, but I pose as being a reasonably fair farmer. I believe that we farmers have to some extent been blameful ourselves, that we have not been doing everything we cculd in the way of bringing wool to the market in good shape, and I believe also that the manufacturers could have done more than they have done.
But there are incidental gains in sheep raising that should not be lost sight of. For instance, there is the extermination of weeds. The Minister of Agriculture, a farmer like myself though probably not such a tiller of the soil, will appreciate that sheep will do more than all the men you can employ to exterminate weeds. Then, there is the renewal of the fertility of the soil by raising large flocks of sheep. There is also to be considered the very important question of the health of the people. You remember the learned discussion we had here a few weeks ago about preserving the health of the people; the way to do that is for the people to eat more mutton. What makes Britain what she is; it is largely the eating of mutton.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I thought it was roast beef.

- With a little roast beef added occasionally. Somehow or other we don't eat mutton in Canada to the extent they do in other countries. But, I am told by doctors-and I do not care to depend on the doctors, more than I can help, but I have to take their word in this case-I am told by doctors that there is no animal food so good as mutton. There was an inspection of animals in the United States in 1905 and of 8,000,000 sheep examined only 27 were affected with tuberculosis, whereas, of 6,000,000 cattle inspected 11,000 were affected, and of 25,000,000 hogs 207,000 had tuberculosis. For one sheep affected there were 555 cattle and 2,390 hogs, and yet the people will eat pork. I believe that the history of countries similar to Canada, particularly the history of the United States, shows that we can build up a great and profitable woollen industry here. I had intended to read from 'Sheep Husbandry in Canada,' issued by the Department of Agriculture but it wdll take less time if hon. members read it themselves. I believe it is prepared by Dr. Rutherford, anyway it is issued by the department and presumably reliable, and it shows that there are great areas of land in the various provinces fit for raising sheep, and that the conditions in Canada are such as to enable us to establish a large wool producing industry. We have a duty on wool but it seems to be a farce. In 1907 there were 8,000,000 pounds of wool imported, and I am told by those who profess to under-



stand that 6,500,000 pounds of that should have been dutiable, and yet the return brought down by the Minister of Customs shows that we only derived a duty of $6 from all the wool imported into Canada in that year. I want to say as emphatically as I can that even at this late hour the government should do something to prevent the wool growing and the wool manufacturing industries from being wiped out. There is no doubt in my mind, there is no doubt in the mind of any thoughtful person, there is no doubt in the mind of any one who studies the conditions, that we can build up in Canada an enormous industry in the production of wool and in the conversion of that wool into clothing. And, although the quantity we are exporting at present is not very large because our total clip of wool is only 12,000,000 pounds, yet we can increase it so enormously that we can practically clothe our own people with wool grown in our own country. I do think it is high time for the government to cease jollying these two great industries. The government is trying to satisfy them with empty statements every time these people come to Ottawa, and yet the government does nothing. I want to read a line or two from an eloquent speech delivered by the right hon. the Prime Minister-the right hon. gentleman's speeches are always eloquent and graceful-at the Manufacturers' banquet in Montreal last year when the elections were coming on. He said:
Their argument is that if the quality of British goods were equal to the quality of Canadian goods they could compete, but they say, that under the tariff the British manufacturer is able to send to Canada a certain class of article which is inferior in quality, though shining in appearance, and seductive to the customer, but worth less than the money he pays for it; in other words, that the goods which are sent over from Great Britain to Canada are shoddy goods, made up of a little wool and a good deal of tops and oil and waste, cobwebs and refuse, and similar things, which are given to the innocent Canadian consumer.
I want the House to note particularly how they are made up-of cobwebs and refuse and similar things-because of the advice my right hon. friend afterwards gives. Summing up, he said:
If, after all, the man or woman, deluded or not deluded, chooses to buy the cheap shining goods, why, in the name of everything that is proper, do you not give him or her the cheap shining goods? Why is it that you cannot produce what is produced by the British manufacturer? Well, sir, if it be that the conscience of the Canadian manufacturer is too severe, that they will give only pure wool and nothing else, I say that is not business.
That is the advice my right hon. friend gives to the manufacturers and the people Mr. LENNOX.
of Canada; and he opens that speech by saying that he is going to have a heart-to-heart talk with them. The heart-to-heart talk, all boiled down, is this: The British manufacturers unload these goods, made partly of wool, but considerably of cobwebs and refuse; you the Canadian manufacturers should adapt yourselves to the conditions, go into the same line of business, and when the innocent Canadian consumer, deluded or not deluded, comes to buy, give him the cheap shining stuff, and if your conscience is too severe for that, all I have to say is, ' that is not business.'

Mr. Speaker, as a new member of this ' House, I crave the indulgence of the members for a short time while 1 discuss this question in which I am so very much interested. The remarks which I have to make may not be clothed in that grammatical form which is familiar to hon. members on both sides, owing to the fact that I have not been blessed with a college education nor with a grammar school education, nor even with an ordinary common 'school education. I have had to earn my living since before I was ten years of age; so that if the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) is a fair specimen of the farming community of this c untry, I claim to be a fair specimen of the working men of this country. Now, Mr. Speaker, the remarks which I have to make refer to a very large number of the worKmg men, the working women, the working boys and the working girls of Canada who are engaged in the woollen industry. My remarks are not made from a theoretical standpoint or from what I have heard or read, but they are made from 28 years of hard practical experience. I have been here on several deputations to this government asking for a revision of the woollen tariff. I do not know whether the hon. Finance Minister is going to ask me before I am through what it is we want: if he is, I will answer him to the best of my ability. Although several deputations on behalf of the woollen industry have waited on the government during recent years, nothing has been done by the government other than to send to Great Britain a commissioner to investigate the causes of the difference in cost of manufacture in Great Britain and in Canada. I have the report of that commissioner, and I will say on behalf of the woollen manufacturers of Canada that we are thankful that the government have done even that much, because if they take the trouble to examine this report, they will realize the great disadvantage under which the Canadian woollen manufacturers labour as compared with the woollen manufacturers of Great Britain. The report is addressed to Mr. John Me-

Dougald, Commissioner of Customs, Ottawa, Canada, and it says:
Inclosed herewith is a complete list of wages that are now being paid in the districts of Bradford, Leeds and Huddersfield to operatives in the manufacture of woollens and worsteds, when paid by the days or by the week.
After going very fully into the cost of the various branches of manufacture, the report says:
In order to make a comparison between the cost of manufacturing in Canada and in Great Britain, it would, in my opinion, be necessary to take into account the following items: 1, wages; 2 more expensive factory buildings; 3, extra cost of heating; 4, additional buildings; 5, extra capital employed in carrying larger stocks; 6, higher rate of interest on money; 7, increased cost of machinery; 8, more expensive motive power; 9, owing to Canadian mills having a limited market, they are compelled to show a large number of designs each season, and manufacture from comparatively short warps, which interferes with production and increases cost; 10, the specialization which is so general in Yorkshire has many advantages in lowering the cost of production.
In order to ascertain the actual difference in the cost of producing goods in Great Britain and in Canada, I have gone to the trouble of getting comparisons of five of the principal items enumerated in this list: 1, wages; 2, higher rate of interest charged in Canada as compared with Great Britain; 3, extra cost of fuel; 4, more expensive factory buildings; 5, increased cost of machinery. I took that report to a woollen manufacturer, who has a factory similar in size to the one on which the commissioner apparently based this report, that is, a ten-set mill, or one with ten sets of cards. I took it to the Rosamond woollen company mill of Almonte, which is conducted on the best principles, a mill whose exhibit of tweeds at the Centennial Exhibition in Philadelphia captured the gold medal against all American competition.
A woollen mill is divided into some eight or ten different parts. I have taken the five principal parts and made a comparison in respect of these between the factories in Great Britain and those in Canada. There are what we call the dye-house, the scouring plant, the carding room, the spinning room, the weaving and finishing room. These are the five principal rooms. While there are several others, these are the most important and are the ones with respect to the operation of which I have compared the prices. Here are the wages given by the commissioner, whom we sent to England, as paid in Great Britain and those paid for similar help in Canada. First, take the dye house. In Britain the overseers receive $12.16 per week. In Canada 1314
we pay them $20 per week. In England, the labourers who work under .the overseers, receive from $5.16 to $7 per week. In this country we pay them $8 per week. In the carding room, the overseers in Britain are paid from $14.60 to $17.04 a week and in this country they get $24 per week. Their under help receive in Britain $6 per week and in this country $8. The women and girls employed in those rooms receive in Britain $3.65 per week and we pay them $6.16. In the spinning department, the overseers receive on the otheT side $9.73 a week and in. this country $18 per week. The men working under them receive $3.40 per w'eek in Britain as compared with $7.40 per week in this country. In the weaving department, the overseers receive in Britain from $12.16 to $13.38 per wTeek and we pay them $18. Their assistants get on the other side $4.87 to $6.33 per week as compared with $11.20 on this side. In the finishing denartment, the overseers in Britain receive $8.52 to $9.73 per week and we pay them $18. The boys and girls in the different departments in the finishing room, receive in Britain from $2.43 to $2.92 per week, whereas we pay them from $5.40 to $6.16. Then the mechanics are paid in Britain $8.36 per week whereas here they get $10.12.
Those are the differences in wages paid in the five principal branches in a woollen mill, comparing the two countries. A very important question, to my mind, was to find out what difference that would make, comparing a mill of this country with one of similar size in the old land. I asked the Rosamond Woollen Mill Company if they would kindly let me know what their annual pay-roll amounted to. They replied that it amounted to $82,000 per annum, exclusive of office help. The difference in the rates of wages between the two countries, taking it at a very low average, would amount to 50 per cent in favour of the mother country, and in that average I think I am rather under the estimate according to the commissioner's report. How does that work out in a mill, the size of the one I have referred to? The Rosamond Woollen Company pay $82,000 in wages per annum. A mill of similar size in the old country would pay only $55,000 per annum. In other words if you add 50 per cent to the $55,000 you have $82,000. So that a mill of the size of the Rosamond Woollen Mill in Canada is paying $27,000 a year more in wages than a mill of similar size in Great Britain.
The next item that struck me is the difference in the cost of money in Canada as compared with Great Britain. Nobody knows that difference better than the hon. the Minister of Finance. When I say that it takes a pretty solid industry in Canada to get money at 6 per cent, 1 am putting the rate as low as possible. How does that compare with the rate in Great Britain? I

have had money myself in an indirect way on goods shipped to this country, sold strictly on a cash basis, from the time the goods were shipped until the money was paid, and I was charged a rate of 2i per cent per annum. But I am basing my calculations on a rate of 4 per cent in the old country, which I think is reasonable compared with 6 per cent in Canada. How does that work out in a plant the size of the one I have referred to? They have in use in that concern no less than half a million dollars, which, at 6 per cent, gives $30,000 interest per annum. A concern requiring the same amount of money in the old country can get it at 4 per cent or $20,000 interest, would have to pay $20,000 in interest, showing a difference against the Canadian manufacturer, in the case of a mill of similar size, of $10,000 per annum. The next item is the cost of fuel. In the old country, fuel costs exactly one-half, perhaps a little less, what it does in this country. A mill, such as the one I have referred to, uses $6,000 worth of fuel in a year. A mill of similar size in the old country will consume $3,000 worth of fuel. In other words it costs the Canadian manufacturer $3,000 more for fuel than it does the British manufacturer and he has to use more. The next item is the cost of buildings and machinery. Let me cite an actual occurrence. A couple of years ago the Rosamond Woollen Company advertised for tenders for the erection of a large weaving shed. The building was to be a large one of either brick or stone covered with iron. The lowest tender was $28,000, and the parties thought the price so enormous that they gave up the idea of erecting the building. Shortly afterwards^ one of the members of the firm had occasion to visit the old country for the purpose of purchasing some woollen machinery. While there in" conversation with some manufacturers, he happened to refer to the building of this weaving shed. They asked him to submit plans and they would get an estimate. He gave them the dimensions, and to his utter astonishment, the estimated cost was $18,000 for a building for the construction of which $28,000 was the lowest bid on this side. That makes a difference between the two of 55 per cent. How does that apply to a plant similar to the one I have referred to? *The cost of the building in that town was $130,000-a magnificent stone building, no better in the Dominion for its size." But in the old country a building of the same proportions would cost 55 per .cent cheaper.
In other words, a building that, in this country, would cost $130,000 could be built m the old country for $84,000. There is the difference in that item alone, of $46,000. The interest on_ this^ amount is $2,760 a year. The next item is the machinery. In that plant, the machinery cost $150,000. I' Mr. THOBURN.
think there is about 37i or 38 per cent dif-fernce in the cost of machinery in Canada as compared with the old country. It may not be quite that now, but at the time these mills were supplied with machinery the difference was actually greater, the Canadian manufacturer has to pay for cases and freight delivered to Liverpool from the place of manufacture 121 per cent, and when you add whatever duty there is and freight, it makes it, I think, not far from the figure I have given. Take this plant of $150,000 and deduct 371 per cent, and you get $106,000. In other words, it costs $44,000 more to supply a mill of this size with machinery in Canada than it does in Great Britain. The interest on $44,000 is $2,640. So, with $46,000 extra for the building, and $44,000 extra for machinery, you have $90,000 as the added cost of such an establishment in Canada over the cost of a similar establishment in Great Britain. In summing up the annual expenditure, the difference in wages, the difference in the rate of interest, the difference in cost of fuel, the difference in interest charge because of extra cost of building and machinery, we find a total of $45,400. That is the amount, in round figures, which it costs the manufacturer in this country to run a mill like that in Almonte more than it would cost to operate a similar mill in Great Britain.
Now, there has been a good deal said in this country about inferior machinery. We are told that it is because the Canadian manufacturer has inferior machinery that he cannot produce cloth as cheap or as good as the manufacturer in the old country produces. I deny that charge, and I speak from experience. I venture to say that, in proportion to the machinery we have in operation in Canada to-day, we have just as good machinery if not better, than they have in Great Britain. And I would like nothing better than to have the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson), and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) visit the manufacturing town of Almonte and see if what I say with reference to machinery is not correct. These gentlemen may say:	There is no
use in our going there, because we are not judges of woollen machinery. I meet that argument by asking them to bring with them the best expert woollen manufacturer they can find in the Dominion of Canada, and see if he does not bear out my statement with reference to the character of woollen machinery used in this country.
Now, Mr. Speaker, you can understand, from the figures I have given, how difficult it is for the manufacturers in Canada to compete with the manufacturers in Great Britain. I do not know whether

any of the hon. members opposite have ever visited the manufacturing districts of Great Britain; but I have done so, and I know that it is a sorry sight to see the operatives coming out of these woollen mills, wearing wooden shoes and with shawls over their heads, not as well clad as the squaws of our country are. Compare this with the manner in which our operatives are clothed; compare the homes of these people in Bradford and other manufacturing districts in Great Britain with the homes of the workers in woollen mills in Canada, and I do not think any member of this House would wish to see our operatives compelled to live in such homes as those occupied by the operatives of these great manufacturing districts in Great Britain. But I can say this also, give the Canadian working man the same chances as those enjoyed by the working man in the old country and he will produce goods faster and I think better. For some reason or other, we have to work faster in this country than they work in the old country. What the reasons may be, it is a little difficult to say, but I know, from what I have seen, that the fact is as I state. Possibly, some of the hon. members opposite, or some on this side of the House have travelled in Great Britain. If so, they can hardly help having noticed that the manner of working there is much slower than it is in this country. I went through Great Britain once in the harvest time, and I saw more help in one harvest field there than you would find in five harvest fields in this country. Help is so cheap that there is no difficulty in getting abundance of it. _ One of the most amazing things- speaking from a Canadian standpoint-I saw in travelling through the British agricultural districts was a man ploughing in the field driving three horses, tandem. I suppose every Canadian will know what I mean when I say ' tandem,' with two boys leading the horses. To the Canadian eye, nothing could be much more ridiculous. I will guarantee to take a Canadian boy of seventeen years old, put him behind the plough with a span of horses, and he will do more work in a day than that man was doing with his three horses and two boys. There is the difference between the workman in Canada and the workman in Great Britain.

I should be sorry to interfere with the course of the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Thoburn) argument, for, I know this is his maiden speech, and he is speaking well. But, if he will permit me a question at this point, I would ask whether he has taken into calculation the very element of which he speaks ? The figures he gave were based on the weekly wages here and
in England. Does the Canadian manufacturer, with double the wages, get double the product out of his operatives? Does the hon. gentleman see what I mean ?
No, I do not quite catch it.

I understand the hon. gentleman's argument to be that a Canadian workman will produce far more work in a certain number of hours than an English workman will produce. The hon. gentleman's comparison, I think, was with reference to the weekly wages of the operative in Canada and the operative in England. That has a bearing on the case because if the Englishman who gets 36 a week turns out, we will say, 10 yards while the Canadian who receives $12 a week turns out 20 yards, the product is the same as far as labour is concerned.

Such a difference is an utter impossibility because the product of an employee in a woollen factory is principally turned out by machinery; it is not the same as two labourers working in competition; it would be impossible to get the machine to turn out double the quantity in this country that it would in England.
The machine runs at the same rate in England as it does here.
Then the difference in wages is nothing.

There is little hand work in a woollen mill, it is practically all machine work. I was struck by an item which I read in the 'Glasgow News' in reference to our Canadian athletes. In discussing the Canadian curlers, it said:
One cannot attempt to explain away the Canadian superiority. These are the real wizards of the game. The Canadian curler is the product of the Canadian climate and he cannot be produced north of the Tweed.
Whatever applies to the Canadian athe-lete as the result of our climate, applies in every sense of the word to the Canadian workman. Give the Canadian workman the same chance as the workman of Great Britain and I think he will defy the world as to the quality and the quantity of the work he will turn out.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What does the hon. gentleman mean when he says to give the Canadian workman the same chance? I do not want to interrupt my hon. friend who is speaking with great interest and with a knowledge of the subject, but what does the Canadian workman lack?

He lacks labour. All I ask the Finance Minister is to give labour and that is all the Canadian workman is asking for. It is on their behalf that I plead this afternoon, on behalf of
