the thousands of workmen in the woollen industry who are idle.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not see the point of my hon. friend's argument, I confess.

Another mistaken idea is prevalent in this country, that if you increase the duty you will increase the cost of the article to the consumer. That does not always follow. I am not speaking on behalf of woollen manufacturers generally in making this statement but I speak on my own behalf. I am not so very anxious whether I get an increased price for the article I am producing; all I am begging for is a market for the article I am producing. Let me illustrate. Supposing that one of the ministers was engaged in manufacturing, that he had a firm producing $1,000,000 worth of goods and that he was making a fair living and a reasonable profit. Then suppose that, say, through the introduction of a preferential clause, $500,000 worth of such goods as; he was producing were allowed to enter this country and to get into the hands of his customers Not because they got any more for the goods than he did, but from the very fact of their coming into this country, they would deprive him of one half of his customers, they would deprive one half of his workmen of their employment and what benefit is derived? That is the point I want to make so far as the increased duty is concerned. The hon. gentleman asks, what are you asking? I have not yet asked an increased duty but that is what I am aiming at, not so much that it will increase the cost of the article but that it will give a market for the goods I am producing. Let us go a little further. Supposing the re-arrangement of the woollen tariff did mean an addition of 5 cents a yard in the cost of the cloth for a suit of clothes-and even one half of five cents a yard would be a handsome profit for a woollen manufacturer who had a large factory. But suppose it did make a difference of five cents a yard, what difference would that make to the man buying a suit of clothes? Just 35 cents. How many men in Canada would object to paying 35 cents extra for a suit of clothes provided you give all the men in this country plenty of work? Not one in the whole Dominion. It would be almost a calamity to the people of Canada if they had to depend entirely upon foreign woollen manufacturers. We know from experience that when all Canadian factories of any kind are closed the cost of the article is bound to advance. Let me give you an illustration from practical experience. From 1870 to 1880 I was engaged in mercantile business and hon. members will remember that at that time the burning question was the tariff on sugar. There were only one or two sugar refineries in Canada but thev were producing a first Mr. THOBUEN.
class article. The wily government of the United States, in an effort to close out that industry in Canada, paid the American sugar refineries an export bounty on sugar. What was the result? In 1877 we had to sell what we called a good article of brown sugar at 10 cents a pound and we thought we were selling it cheap. We sold it at 10 cents so long as there was competition between tha Canadian manufacturer and the American manufacturer. The Canadian manufacturers waited on the government again and again in an effort to have that tariff so arranged that they could compete with the American manufacturer who was receiving an export bounty, but they could get no redress from the government of that day, and not a single Canadian refinery continued running, they had to close their doors. What was the result? It was utterly impossible for us' to sell a pound of brown sugar at that time for less than 12i cents. It may be a matter of surprise to hon. members of this House perhaps to know that only so recently as 1877 they paid 121 cents a pound for brown sugar. But, such is the fact.
And after the duty was put on it was sold at from four to five cents a pound?

Yes. You know what the prices have been since you have had good healthy competition. So much with reference to competition in the manufacture of woollen goods. My contention has always been that the Canadian manufacturer is as great a benefit to the Canadian farmer as it is possible for one interest to be a benefit to another. I do not know that I was ever more interested in listening to a speech than I was the other night when the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) was advocating so zealously and so well the protection of the Nova Scotia coal mines. I thought, Sir, that that was one of the most patriotic speeches, one of the best speeches from a protectionist standpoint that I have heard for a long time, and I can only say that if it were to come to a vote in this House, although I am a consumer of coal in my business, I would not stand up in my place only once, but I would stand up twice, and, if the Speaker would allow me, I would stand up three times to vote with the hon. member for Cape Breton. Let me quote a few of his words:
While it is the interest of this country that capital should be safeguarded and capitalists the world over be given the assurance that in Canada we have a parliament and parliamentarians who always keep their eye upon the best interests of those who are willing to invest their capital in this country it is equally in our interest that we should likewise keep in mind the men, women and children who are dependent upon this particular industry in

every part of Canada, and in doing this we are likewise improving the position of those who invest capital in Canadian industries.
I would like to ask, Mr. Speaker, if there is anything more applicable to the Canadian woollen industry than these words as applied to the Nova Scotia miners? Then he goes on:
I would submit, Sir, that while it may he a hardship in some eases to buy coal, as we sometimes consider it dearer than we would like to pay, we should not forget that the people of the great country to the south of us have pursued the policy which I am advocating. The people in the New England states have no coal, they have to receive their coal from the west and they pay a higher price than they would have to pay for Nova Scotia coal. Still, there is enough national spirit-
That is what I like to hear.
-to induce them to bear with any little extras they would have to pay in order to develop in the west great coal centres and keep the trade within their own bounds.
I could not use language as eloquent as that in behalf of the Canadian woollen manufacturers. I only wish I could, but I am quoting the hon. gentleman's words to help me in my argument. Then:
I regret that this winter they have not been kept in continuous employment

Referring to the employees engaged in the Nova Scotia coal mines.
-because of this displacement of Canadian coal in the home market by American coal.
I regret exceedingly that the woollen operatives in the manufacturing centres of the Dominion of Canada are not employed continuously and that a great number of them were not employed at all during the winter months through which we have just passed. But, Sir, further on he says in closing his address:
I have presented my views and these statistics to the House in the hope that the government will take into serious consideration the circumstances of those who are dependent on this trade for a means of livelihood as well as those who have had the courage and the enterprise to invest millions of dollars in the development of our coal areas in Nova Scotia and elsewhere in Canada.
That is what I am asking the government to do. I am asking, the government to take into consideration the men who have invested their millions of dollars in the woollen industries of this country. I was pleased with the reply the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) made. He said:
I do not imagine that my hon. friend (Mr. McKenzie) desires to divide the House on this question to-night, especially as there is a very slim attendance of members present. 1 take it for granted that the purpose of his motion was to have an opportunity of presenting these very interesting statistics to us
and to urge, if it be necessary to urge, the importance of this great mining^ industry. There will be no difference of opinion in that respect.
I hope and trust that there will be no difference of opinion between the hon. Minister of Finance, the Minister of Customs and myself with reference to this great woollen industry. It seems to me that every man in this House, irrespective of politics, is a national policy man, is a protectionist, when it is touching anything in which he is personally interested. Not only did I read with pleasure the speech of the hon. member for Cape Breton, but I have noticed the following proposed resolution by the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Sealy) on the Order Paper:
That in the opinion of this House, so long as the Canadian tariff affords, incidentally or otherwise, a considerable degree of protection to manufacturers, some protection may fairly and properly be afforded by our tariff to Canadian agriculturists and stock raisers upon hogs, hog products, garden vegetables and such other items as it may appear possible to so protect with advantage to the agriculturist, and without undue injury to the Canadian consumer.
With reference to the very items that the hon. gentleman proposes to have protected, to my certain knowledge, no greater protection could be given to the Canadian farmer than that which he would secure by establishing and maintaining the woollen industries of this country. I know for a fact that in the town in which I live, the town of Almonte, the woollen manufacturers have paid out millions and millions of dollars for farm products, a laTge portion of which would not otherwise have been sold at all, it would have gone to waste. They have paid for wood alone, which in the early days would have been burnt in log piles, millions and millions of dollars. They have paid millions and milions of dollars to the farmers for the product of their orchard and gardens which could not be exported from this country. I claim that the manufacturers are as great a benefit to the farmer as it is possible for them to be from the fact that they buy such a large quantity of the products of the farm that cannot possibly be exported.
There aTe thousands and thousands of farmers in this country who cannot raise grain for export and who make out of the manufacturing industries of this country a living which in their absence they could not make. Speaking from the standpoint of a woollen manufacturer, and I know whereof I speak, I would ask the Minister of Agriculture if there is any branch of agriculture more profitable to the farmer than sheep raising? Let me give an illustration of that. Take a farmer having 100 sheep and at the very lowest estimate there would be 100 lambs. . In our neighbourhood last year the lambs

sold for $5 each, giving the farmer $500, and the lowest calculation would be one dollar's worth of wool for each sheep, giving another $100 or $600 in all, from the 100 sheep. Does the Minister of Agriculture think there is any other branch of farming which will give the farmer the same return for such a small capital invested and such small labour as would be bestowed on these 100 sheep? The hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) dealt with the question as to the price of wool very lucidly and very ably, and I quote from the Montreal Trade Bulletin of a few days ago the following:
Canadian Wool and the Tariff.
The present tariff is about as discouraging recently at 12c. to 13c. About fifteen or he can get for his washed fleece in the west, is about 14c. to 15c., whilst we hear of sales recently at 12c. to 13c. About fifteen or eighteen months ago the farmer was getting from 27c. to 28c. for his washed fleece, whilst to-day he has to be content with the unprofitable returns of those figures cut in two; and the grim irony of the whole thing at present is, that our farmers are mainly dependent upon the highly protected American market as an outlet for his product. The tariff is not affording the farmers a chance to raise wool profitably, nor have the manufacturers a fair show to compete with foreign goods.
Let me give to the House an illustration of the fluctuations in the price of wool in say a period of 12 months. It may be a surprise to a goodly number of you to know that from our own Northwest Territories there come annually about 1,300,000 pounds of wool. The sheep industry is only in its infancy in that country. I am engaged in a woollen business in which I use exclusively almost Northwest wool, and I am proud to say, whatever the cause of it may be, they produce in the Northwest Territories a quality of wool such as cannot be produced in any other part of the Dominion. Until I commenced to use the Canadian Northwest wool I was using wool imported from the Cape of Good Hope, and to the credit, of our own northwestern farmers be it said that they are now raising a wool nearer the texture of -what we call fine Cape wool than we have been able to get from any other part of Canada. A shoTt time ago the price of that wool was 20 cents a pound, and the 1,300,000 pounds brought to the farmers $260,000, but this year the price of wool is 14 cents per pound, or less, and on the same basis of production it would only bring $182,000 or a loss in one year to the farmers of Saskatchewan and Alberta of $78,000. Why does this state of things exist? I -will tell you, and in doing so I will have to treat of a personal matter. The principal mills using that class of wool in Canada were the flannel mills, one of which I own and operate. The personal aspect of the case is this, and it is something that Mr. THOBURN.
affects me and you cannot blame me for referring to it-when the government saw fit some years ago to insert that preferential clause in the woollen tariff T had no doubt that their idea was a good one and possibly the government expected that by giving that preference Great Britain would give us something in return. But, Sir, so far as I know Great Britain has never given us one dollar in return. On the other hand I will tell you what that preference has done for us. It has allowed millions and million dollars worth of manufactured' goods to ccme into the country that were not coming in before. It has taken millions of dollars of wages out of the pockets of the working man, and the working woman, and the working boy, and the working girl of Canada and placed it in the pockets of the working classes of Great Britain. Let me bring the question still nearer home to myself. When, some years ago, for reasons best known to themselves the government changed that tariff, and restored part of the preference to tweed manufacturies, but they discriminated against the manufacturers of flannels and blankets. I now appeal personally to the Prime Minister, because I think from the very bottom of my heart that if he takes this matter in hand he will have it rectified. Nor am I speaking now so much for myself as for the Canadian woollen industry generally. The point I want to make is this: the flannel manufacturers of this country have been fighting with the whole force of that preferential clause against them, and I have come down here more than once with other flannel manufacturers and waited upon the government, and we thought we were not asking any favour, for all we asked was to be put on the same footings as other woollen manufacturers, we being woollen manufacturers in every sensg of the word. But, for some reason or other our request was never granted. And what has been the result? Two flannel mills in my own town have closed down, and the demand for that Northwestern wool has fallen off, and the loss has amounted to a sum of $78,000. I cannot make my statement any plainer. I can only say in conclusion that I have seen the day, before I was a manufacturer of woollen goods, when we paid in Ontario as high as 52 cents a pound for Canadian wool. It may be a surprise to many members of this House to hear that, but it is a fact. In those days all the small mills in Canada were in operation and they were using Canadian wool. But, unfortunately, goods not anything like equal in quality, came into this country and from time to time these smaller mills which use the Canadian wool were forced out of existence so that to-day there is hardly a small mill in the Dominion. From 52 cents per pound the price of Canadian wool has gradually decreased, and I say right here, and I am glad I did not

forget it, that no fine wool imported into the Dominion of Canada has decreased in price in the same ratio as has Canadian wool. I can come to no other conclusion than that the reason for that is that we have closed up the mills in this country that were using Canadian wool :	It is worth to-day only
from 12 to 16 cents as compared with 52 cents a few years ago.
Now, I am thankful to the members of this House for the very kind attention they have paid to my remarks. I do earnestly beseech of the government to rearrange the woollen tariff, by increasing the ad valorem duty a little, and by putting a specific duty on the shoddy goods coining to this country, so as to give some relief to the working class for whom I am pleading this afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to know that we are all learning. I was not aware until this afternoon that the hon.
member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) was a farmer, or that the hon. member for North Lanark (Mr. Thoburn) was a labouring man. The woollen question is a very important question. I have been engaged in the woollen industry all my life. I do not claim to be a manufacturer; I have simply been a labourer in the woollen industry from the bottom to the top. We cannot at the present time manufacture in Canada all the classes of woollen goods that we import; but there are certain classes of those goods that we can manufacture. Last year we .imported $20,962,753 worth of woollen goods. I claim that we could have manufactured about half of that in Canada. The question always comes up, does the consumer pay the duty? I claim that he does not always. Previous to 1878, during the time of the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie's government, we had a duty of only 174 per cent, on woollen cloth, and in those days we received for staple goods, six-quarter, fifty-four inches wide, from $1.45 to $1.50 a yard. In 1885, after the National Policy had been in effect for some years, we sold the same class of goods, made from the same class of material, at from 90 to 95 cents a yard.
Can the hon. gentleman tell us what the farmers got for their wool in 1878?
For the class of goods I speak of we were not using wool grown in this country.
The farmers were raising it.

The goods I am talking about were made from imported wool. All-wool gray flannels, 28 inches wide, sold previous to 1878 at from 37i to 40 cents a
yard; in 1885 the same goods sold at from 28 to 30 cents. Navy blue flannel, 28 inches wide, which sold previous to 1878 at from 42i to 45 cents a yard, sold in the years from 1885 to 1889 at from 30 to 32i cents a yard. You may wonder why we were able to sell these goods at these prices. It was because we '^virtually had the Canadian market to ourselves, under the duty of 30 per cent ad valorem on cloth, and the specific duty of 10 cents a pound. Every machine in the mill was run to its utmost capacity, the demand was so good. From 1885 to 1889 I was managing a ten-set mill, the output of which amounted to from $260,000 to $275,000 annually. In 1901 and 1902 the annual output of the same plant dropped down to $160,000-why? Because foreign goods were allowed to come in more fully and there was a diminished demand, and every machine was not run to its utmost capacity. Now, there has been a great deal said about shoddy goods. I think it would be better for the people at large if shoddy goods were barred altogether from coming to this country. Shoddy is made from mungo, and in many cases from the filthiest rags that can be picked up. Disease has been brought to this country in shoddy. In the districts in England where shoddy goods are made, you will find the people who labour .in the shoddy mills diseased from head to foot, because they are always working among mungo and filthy rags. If a man who wears shoddy goods visits his neighbour on a cold winter night and sits near the stove, his clothes will smell like a filthy oil barrel. I hope the manufacturers of this country will never be compelled to manufacture this class of goods. With regard to Northwest wool, I had the honour of being the first manufacturer in the province of Ontario to use it, and I wish to say that that country is adapted to the raising of fine wool, as good wool as can be raised in the Cape of Good Hope or in Australia or in Montevideo, and it would be of great benefit to the farmers of the Northwest if there were a market for it. I remember when we paid from 15 to 16 cents a pound for what we called half-breed wool, and from it made beautiful tweeds, of about twenty-ounce weight, which we sold foT 80 cents a yard, and1 there was a good demand for it. We have at the present time a duty of 30 per cent on cloth. I would not advocate increasing that duty, but I would put on a specific duty to keep out shoddy goods. There are mills in England which manufacture these shoddy goods from January to January, and there are other mills which run on doeskins or broadcloth all the year around, without a change. They do that because they have an immense market. We could not do it here, because our market is small at present. But if we encourage manufacturing in our

own country, our home market will become larger. To show the value of a manufacturing plant, I may say that when the Trent Valley Mill was established 28 years ago in the town of Campbellford, where I live, the town had a population of 1,100; now it has a population of 3,000. During that time the mill has paid out in wages $1,000,000, and although the town gave it a bonus of $10,000 and exemption from taxes for ten years, ithas during that~time paid $30,000 of taxes, not to speak of the taxes paid by the employees.
You can see the benefit which that plant has been to the town of Campbellford. It has increased the population of that little village from 1,100 to 3,000 souls. Campbellford is the market town of East Northumberland. The farmers drive there with their vegetables, and no man ever came to the town of Campbellford and went away with his load unsold. That is because the people there are employed in its manufacturing establishments, and it is they who buy the products of the farm to a very great extent. In every town where there is a large manufacturing establishment you have a great market for the country miles around. Campbellford is the market town for East Northumberland. I shall not take up more time, as my hon. friend from Simcoe Mr. Lennox) and my hon. friend from North Lanark (Mr. Tho-burn), have very well covered the ground, but I wish merely to raise my voice on behalf of a little more protection for our woollen industries, that is if you wish to keep them in the country. Many woollen mills have gone to the wall and millions of dollars have been wasted, and it has been proven that during the years when the national policy was in existence, woollen clothes were cheaper to the consumer than they are to-day or than they were previous to 1878. So that I think that in protecting our manufacturers, we are protecting our farmers. The farmer is the bone and sinew of the country, he is the great producer, but the farmer and the manufacturer must go hand in hand. The one cannot get along very well without the other. Let me point out that we are building through my riding the Trent Valley canal, which is bound to develop thousands of electric horse-power in the near future, and we want manufacturers to come and locate their establishments along the canal banks. Our people are looking forward to seeing city after city on the banks of the Trent Valley canal, but we need a little more protection before we can hope for any increase in the number of our manufacturing establishments. I hope the government will give this matter their earnest consideration; and if they do, they cannot but come to the conclusion that the woollen industry should have a little more protection than is now given it.

I propose, Mr. Speaker, to take up but briefly the time of the House in discussing this very important subject. Having listened with great interest to the speakers in favour of the resolution, it seems to me that the question before us is that of revivifying the old national policy. It is again the question of higher protection and bolstering up manufacturing industries. I ask if that is really the principle on which our national prosperity depends. My hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) and from North Lanark (Mr. Thoburn) tried somewhat to disguise the situation. They came before the House, the one as a ' farmer and the other as a labourer, and each wanted something done for the particular class of which he posed as a champion. But I am in the judgment of the House if the whole burden of their song was not a plea for special legislation on behalf of a special class, and of a class which seems to be doing, to say the least, as well as the average farmer. We were, wont to think of my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) as a lawyer, and consequently might feel justified in regarding any argument from him as not altogether disinterested and consequently open to suspicion, but when we now find him posing on the floor of this House as a farmer,
I presume we must necessarily take him at his word. But at the same time I cannot see that his argument for the farmer was as strong or convincing as he would like to have it. The fact of my hon. friend declaring that the proposition before the chair would be beneficial to the farmer is not proof. His whole argument must be based on the sunnosition that an increase in the protection to this particular manufacturing industry would mean the payment to the farmer of higher prices for his wool. But how would our farmers be paid higher prices for their wool unless you shut out foreign competition? So that we have my hon. friend practically pleading for a duty on wool. On the other hand the hon. member for North Lanark (Mr. Thoburn) speaks more particularly as a manufacturer, and as such a condition of things beneficial to him must be a cheap raw product and a dear manufactured product.
Not necessarily.

That must be the condition if he is going to increase his production. The manufacturer wants protection. For what purpose? My hon. friend says to preserve the home market. But that must necessarily be, to a large extent at least, a subterfuge, because the thing he really wants is to shut out the finished foreign product from coming into competition with his own. There we have the old anomaly of protection. When you increase

protection on the raw material, you must end by increasing it on the manufactured product, and thereby necessarily leave the farmer in the same position as before. If the argument of my hon. friend from Sim-coe as a farmer, and that of my hon. friend from North Lanark as a manufacturer, obtain, I cannot see how the farmer is going to be benefited. The benefit to the farmer, as outlined by the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), resolves itself into this, namely, that the increased demand for the raw material by the manufacturer, would necessarily benefit the farmer. But it must not be forgotten that in this country we have a rather rigorous climate which necessitates our purchasing large quantities of prepared woollen goods. Now the mere pittance which an increase in the tariff would give the producer of the raw material would be more than swamped by the extra amount he would have to pay for the prepared article. On behalf of the people in my county, I say that it is not the duty of the government to make it hard for the people who are struggling for an existence to buy the necessaries of life. It is not on these articles of woollen clothing that our present tariff should be made higher. At present we have a duty of 30 to 35 per cent on these prepared articles, and it seems to me that in exacting that duty we are bolstering up pretty well and taking pretty good care of our manufacturers. Since these hon. gentlemen appear so anxious on behalf of the labourer and the farmer, I would ask them if the living conditions of the average farmer on a homestead compare in any way, as regards luxuries and advantages of life, with those of the manufacturer in the city?
But we are told that our manufactories are the means of supporting a large working population. But the hon. member for North Lanark (Mr. Thoburn) himself pointed out that the conditions of labour in this country are vastly in advance of those in the old country, and he proposes to bring our labouring classes into somewhat the same condition. He wants cheaper labour. The fact is that every man who wants protection for his particular industry and who has some personal and peculiar advantage to gain by taxing other people, is in favour of the national policy. I do not believe it is a ' national ' policy to support any particular class to the disadvantage of the great classes. I do not believe in raising the tariff for the sake of protecting an industry whose decadence-assuming that it is going backward-is due to the natural conditions that exist. The maintenance of an industry in this country must depend on whether the national resources are sufficient to support that or not?
Will the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Certainly.
What does he think about the bounties on iron and steel?

I am not discussing the bounties on iron and steel.
I am quite willing to give my opinions on that subject at the proper time. There is a rule in this House to the effect that speakers should confine .themselves to the matter under discussion.
What about the duties on agricultural implements?

There is a rule in this House that speakers should confine themselves to the matters under discussion, and we are not discussing the duties on agricultural implements just now. But if he wants my opinion on that subject, I may inform him that I am not in favour of duties on agricultural implements and never have been.

For the information of the hon. membeT for Strathcona (Mr. Wilbert McIntyre) I may say that his Temarks indicate one of the difficulties that have always existed in this discussion-there is such a wide misapprehension of the facts. The hon. gentleman says that he believes the woollen manufacturers have a protection to the extent of 30 or 35 per cent. I want him to understand that I have been struggling under a duty of only 22J per cent.
I understand that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Thoburn) is a manufacturer of blankets.
No.

However
that may be, I believe I am correct in saying that the main articles of woollen manufacture are dutiable to the extent of 30' or 35 per cent.
No.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question? Can he tell us the price of blankets per pound, retail, in Winnipeg?

If the hon. gentleman will ask a question pertaining to what I am discussing I will answer him. I am not a merchant in Winnipeg, as it happens, and I am unable to give him the information he asks for. The point is this: The principle of high protection is one, it seems to me, which we must shun if the development of this country is to be what we desire it to be. We tried high protection for eighteen years, and a pretty bitter trial it was. The hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) says that for eighteen years they have been trying to educate this House how to legislate for prosperity.
Excuse me; I referred to the eighteen years when the party now in power were in opposition and were denouncing the national policy.

I understood the hon .gentleman to say that they were trying to educate this government with regard to the tariff. I can only say that we have had greater prosperity since we changed the tariff than before.
What do you call 'high protection?'

I know that the hon. member (Mr. Hughes) entertains the idea that we still have high protection. So long as he and his friends are happy in that delusion, and we get the benefit of ti e other, I do not see why either of us should complain. The prosperity of this country, in my estimation, depends to a very great extent on the development of western Canada; and I state again, as I have stated before, that when you initiate a policy in this country which increases the cost of the necessaries of life and entails hardship on the people who are developing this country and producing wealth as no other class are, you are stepping aside from the true function of national government. Hon. gentlemen opposite ask us: ' Why not look at this from a national standpoint? ' And yet we find them speaking of this or that particular town or village, or the number of employees engaged in a single manufactory. I am not against manufactures. It is to the interest of the country that manufactures should develop, and .'they will develop naturally as the country develops, and without entailing hardship on the people as a whole. Surely when the farmers of this country have no protection, and when protection means that you put upon the farmers, who are the basis of the wealth of this country, burdens and restrictions, it is time for us to make known our opposition to legislative enactments of that kind. I trust that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) comes to discuss this matter in his budget speech, we shall find that there is no change, or, if there be a change, that it is one toward a lower rather than toward a higher tariff. I think I speak for the majority of the people west of the Great Lakes; I am confident that the people in that part of the Dominion do not want a higher tariff. We have heard it said many times by hon. members on the other side of the House that the future prosperity of this country depends on the prosperity of the country west of the Great Lakes. That being so, it would be clearly unwise for this government, to impose duties which, while possibly benefiting a certain manufacturing town or certain manufacturers, would injure Mr. W. McINTYRE.
the very people to whom we look for the substantial future progress of the country.
May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Wilbert McIntyre) is he in favour of protecting the pork industry?
I may remark to the hon. gentlmean (Mr. Hughes) that the pork industry is not under discussion.

I listened with a great deal of interest to the presentation of the case by my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) and from my hon. friend Mr. Thoburn from North Lanark. The hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Wilbert McIntyre) has endeavoured to leave the impression with the House that -the members on this side who have spoken on this question are in favour of a very high tariff for Canada. For my part, I am in favour of a tariff high enough to keep out of Canada every dollar's worth of goods that we can successfully grow or manufacture in Canada; and I think that it is in the interest of the people that the government of the day, finding that, last year, according to the figures given by my hon. friend from South Simcoe, there was $21,000,000 of woollen goods imported into Canada, the raw material for which could have been grown and the goods themselves manufactured in Canada, should see to it that Canadian interests are taken care of. This should be done by the Minister _ of Finance in the budget which he is to bring down in a few days. I am one of those who believe that it is possible to have a protective tariff that will assure the Canadian manufacturer our own Canadian market, under which consumers will be able to purchase their goods at low prices. If I were to take up the time of the House reviewing the national policy from its introduction in 1879, down to the time when hon. gentlemen opposite came into power in 1896, I am sure I should have no difficulty whatever in proving to the satisfaction of the majority of people of this country that when the national policy was introduced we were importing large quantities of goods from the United States and other countries, and that within a few years factories were established in Canada to manufacture these goods, and yet the goods thus manufactured in Canada were cheaper to the consumer than were those which had been imported before the national policy was introduced.
Mv hon. friend from Strathcona (Mr. W. McIntyre) in his remarks revived an old question. My hon. friend, of course, is not very sincere in his low tariff principles. I am quite sure of that because last year my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Schaffner) introduced a resolution to re-

duce the tariff on agricultural implements from 17i per cent to 10 per cent. Where were my hon. friend's principles then?
Does the hon. gentleman intimate that I voted against that resolution?

My hon. friend thought he would get me into the box of saying that he had voted against that resolution. My hon. friend declares in this House from year to year for a lower tariff to meet, I suppose, the wishes of the farmers of western Canada, and yet when an opportunity presented itself to vote for such a resolution my hon. friend was not in his place and he cannot say that he voted for this resolution. Of course my hon. friend's electors will have their own opinion of that kind of a representative.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: How did my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) vote?

The Finance Minister is not questioning me now, I will have to answer that later. For myself I am not on one side to-day and on another side to morrow. From the moment I took my seat in this House and before that I was a strong advocate of protection for the manu-fecturing and for the farming interests of Canada and I am m the same position to-day. I may say to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) that I have had the honour of moving several resolutions calling for an increase in tariff in the interests of the farmers of Canada.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I had forgotten about the agricultural implements, I was asking for information.

My hon. friend does not require any information from me upon the question of tariff. He understands it very well. The only complaint we have against my hon. friend on that question is not that he does not understand it, but that he fails to act in the interests of the people of Canada. The question before the House is an increase in the tariff that will incidentally help the manufacturer and give him a larger market in this country instead of allowing the market to be supplied by manufactured goads from the United States, Great Britain and other foreign countries. On the other hand my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) has a declaration in the interests of the farmer. Personally I am in favour of both these propositions; I will vote for any resolution that will increase the duty upon the products of the farm and for any reasonable increase of duty upon goods which we can manufacture in Canada that will keep out foreign goods. That is my position, I have always occupied that position and I have no change to make this afternoon.
My hon. friend from Victoria has mentioned the question of pork. I would say to the Finance Minister that during this session he and the first minister have had a large deputation of the swine breeders of Canada asking them to remove the inequality between the Canadian and American tariffs on this question. Whether the hon. Minister of Finance will do that I suppose we will not know for a few days, but while he is considering it may I remind him of the condition of the pork industry in Canada during the past twelve months. The complaint of the swine breeders and farmers-and I think they have a just ground of complaint-is that when the American farmer comes to this country with his pork he is confronted with a duty of two cents a pound; but when the Canadian farmer approaches the border line of the United States he is confronted with a tariff of five .cents a pound, more than double' the Canadian tariff. The Swine Breeders' Association are not complaining particularly about the condition of things in Canada but they feel that they are not being fairly treated. They do not ask for a duty of 5 cents a pound, equal to the American duty, but they do ask that the government should impose a duty of four cents a pound as against five cents in the United States and then the farmers would be quite satisfied with the condition of trade. Surely that is a reasonable request.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My hon. friend's argument is that we should adopt the American rate of duty, or something near it, because it is the American duty. If that is a good argument in relation to pork, is it not equally good for every other item in the American tariff? What is the difference?

The farmers of this country and the gentlemen in this House who agree with me upon this question will expect the Finance Minister to meet the wishes of the farmers. If he does not then he must give up making special appeals for the farmers' votes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The party which appeals to the farmers of this country for the adoption of the American tariff will not receive their approval.

A deputation of my hon. friend's' own political supporters was here the other day asking for this change. A gentleman who was a candidate in my own county a few years ago and who had the honour of a seat in this House for many years, was an ardent free trader in those days, but I noticed that my friend was one of a deputation who asked the government to put a higher protection on pork. What about my hon. friend from Wentworth (Mr. Sea-ley)? I had the honour of hearing my hon. friend up in his county supporting the free trade government, so-called, and when my hon. friend came to this House, a few weeks ago, he placed on the Order Paper a notice, as read by my hon. friend from North Lanark (Mr. Tho-burn) this afternoon, calling for higher protection on pork. My hon. friend is a convert as well. So, on the other side of the House, we have converts to the National Policy. That is the policy I am in favour of myself, the policy that I think is in the best interest of the people of this country. Some of our hon. friends from the west say that they do not want a higher protective tariff. May I suggest that the people of Ontario and eastern Canada are consumers of what they grow in western Canada? In almost every farm house in Ontario there is to be found flour manufactured from wheat grown in western Canada. That is a change that has been brought at out in the last few years. We are not complaining about that. The wheat of western Canada has taken the place of our own wheat. We are quite willing to continue to consume the wheat and flour of western Canada provided it is grown and manufactured in Canada. But, at the same time we think that the people of western Canada should be willing to accept a reasonable protective tariff, so that, instead of the $21,000,000 worth of woollen goods that -jvere imported last year from Great Britain, the United States and other countries, instead of the wages being paid to people in Eng-Mr. BLAIN.
land and foreign countries, the wool might be grown on our own farms, in western Canada if you will, and the wages paid to our own people; so that the operatives, instead of being employed in Great Britain and the United States, might be employed in our own Canadian manufacturing establishments, and so that the farmers of Canada might grow wheat and other cereals to feed the large number of people who would be employed in connection with the woollen industry but who are at the present time out of employment.

I understand they have given notice to reintroduce the Bill. The Bill cannot be dropped from the Order Paper, but why should it be referred back to the committee as it is practically dead?
It has been the custom lately not to proceed in the absence of the hen. member in charge of the Bill.

Explain what the amendments are.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, the only information I have regarding the section which has been added by the Senate, as section 3 of this Bill, is the following:	The company
is anxious to build a line of railway from

Hedleyville to Montmorency river, near the mouth of Laval river; that is to say, over a distance exceeding six miles. That section has been added because, under the Railway Act, the company has no right to build a branch line more than six "miles long. I understand that the distance between these two points is a good deal more than six miles. As regards the second amendment, I would prefer that its consideration be postponed in order that I may obtain the requisite information.
3.	The Canadian Northern Quebec Railway Company may construct a line of railway from a point on its line at or near Hedley ville, thence in a generally easterly direction to a point on the Montmorency river near the mouth of the River Laval. '
4.	The limit to the amount of the securities which the Canadian Northern Quebec Railway Company may issue and secure under* sections 136 to 146 of the Railway Act, both inclusive, shall be a total of thirty thousand dollars per mile of the line hereby authorized and of all lines heretofore authorized to be constructed or constructed by the company or its predecessors by amalgamation, including the amount of the securities heretofore authorized; and such securities may be issued only in proportion to the length of such lines of railway constructed or under contract to be constructed.
Evidently the following new clause has been inserted by the Senate".

As to the first amendment, under the terms of the Railway Act the railway company can construct a branch not longer than six miles, but this branch being more than six miles, power had to be given in the Bill. The hon. gentleman in charge of the Bill has not been informed as to the reason for the other amendments; but he will make inquiry and in the meantime I move the adjournment of the debate.
