Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was urging that the government should increase the tariff on pork coming into this country, in the interest of the Canadian farmer. I notice that when this question
of tariff is up for discussion in the House, hon. members from the west sitting on the government side are continually attempting to set the farmer against the manufacturer; but I believe that when we are protecting the manufacturer we are at the same time protecting the farmer. In my opinion it is impossible to enhance the in-teiest of the one without assisting the interest of the other. In former times during the discussion of the national policy, when our hon. friends opposite were or were supposed to be free traders, attempts were made to array the farmers against the manufacturer and mechanics; but now that cur hon. friends have reluctantly adopted seme measure of protection as their policy, surely it can be said that the whole Canadian people are in favour of the tariff to protect Canadian interests. I am in favour of protection for the farmers of Canada, and I believe that if the Finance Minister were to increase the duty on pork, the $1,000,000 that went out of Canadian pockets last year to United States producers, would be used in purchasing Canadian pork, in the interest of the farmers and all the people of this country. There was a time when the far west and the far east of Canada were separated to a greater extent than they are at present. We have spent large sums of money and given largely of our lands to aid in the construction of railroads between the east and the west. Before these rail-reads were constructed, I could readily understand people in British Columbia favouring a tariff that would allow them to import such products or manufactured goods as they required from the United States; but since we have constructed these lines of railway, I believe that when there is scarcity in any article in one part of Canada, we should supply that article from some other part of Canada rather than import it from the United States. A deputation of market gardeners waited on my hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture a short time ago pointing out that there had been sent last year from the centre of the province of Ontario large quantities of vegetables to Sydney in the province of Nova Scotia. If there is a scarcity in any product, hay for example, in one part of Canada, it is not likely that the same scarcity will be found in every other part of Canada. My hon. friend the Minister of Customs stated this session in answer to a question that there were imported into Canada last year 1,696,115 pounds of blackberries, strawberries, raspberries and gooseberries. Is there a man in this House who would suggest that every dollar's worth of these could not be grown on Canadian farms? Surely there is not. We allow bananas and oranges, which because

oi our climatic conditions cannot be grown in Canada, to come in free of duty, and there will always be sufficient of these to keep the prices of other fruits down to a moderate point in the interest of the consumer. The farmers of Canada realize that wherever there are prosperous towns with manufacturing concerns employing a large number of hands there are good markets for their products, and therefore they have learned that you cannot separate the interest of the farmer from that of the workingman and the manufacturer, that when you are protecting the one you are protecting the other.
The figures given by my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) this afternoon show clearly that the sheep raising industry in this country is diminishing, though we have millions of acres of land well suited for grazing and caring for sheep. Yet, that important industry is diminishing because of the condition of the tariff. I think that is a matter that should engage the very serious attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), who is always a very good listener to statements that are made, but is rather slow to move, even in the interests of the farmers. I think that, *within the last five or six weeks, a golden opportunity has presented itself which, however, this government has allowed to pass. A presidential election was held in the United States a few months ago, the tariff being an important subject of discussion in that election- it is always an important question there as it is here. It was declared by the candidate who was afterwards elected president that a special session of Congress would be called to discuss and revise the tariff. That special session has since been called. That was a golden opportunity for this government to make an effort to have removed some of the inequalities of tariff as between Canada and the United States. I remember the statement made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher)-that, when his party came into power, they would seek and would easily find a greater market for the products of Canadian farmers. One would think that, with such an opportunity as this, the minister would have acted, especially when he finds such inequalities of tariff as these-duty on hay coming into Canada $2 a ton; duty on hay going into the United States $4 a ton; duty on barley coming into Canada, 12 cents per bushel; duty on barley going into the United States, 30 cents per bushel. These inequalities should engage the attention of parliament, and especially of the Minister of Agriculture, whose duty it is to take care of the interests of the farming community. And might I suggest that this would be an important study for the Minister of Customs (Mr. Pater-Mr. BLAIN.
son), for he is a foremost politician in Ontario, and whenever there is a cry for the farmers at election times, he is always ready to appeal for the farmers' vote. In days gone by-days that he has forgotten, no doubt he used to say ;	' What is the use
of duties on farm products ? ' Farmers cannot be protected. When we get into power we will remove the duties.'
I do not remember saying that.
Why, a member of this government, Sir Richard Cartwright, made the statement-

But that is not I.
Mr. BLAIN-that protection is almost equal to highway robbery, and that when his party came into power they would abolish it.
And he is still in the Cabinet.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And my hon. friend's (Mr. Blain) complaint is that we have removed too much of it.

My hon. friend (Mr. Fielding) must not misunderstand me. I am pointing out the attitude of my hon. friend the Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) when he was in opposition and now when he is in the government.
I do not remember saying that.

Of course not. The hon. gentleman does not remember making a charge against the late government, when he was on this side, that it was useless to send a tariff commission throughout the country to find out the condition of trade.
No; I do not remember that.

I quoted the hon. minister's words in this House not_ more than a session or two ago, and I will take the opportunity, before the session closes, if he wishes it, to read to him his very words. He condemns the Liberal-Conservative government for appointing a commission to go up and down the country and find out the condition of trade, but a few years passed and he himself was a prominent member of exactly that kind of a tariff commission.
But they forgot the evidence when they came to report.

Yes, they are always ready to collect evidence, always kept an open dcor to receive deputations, and especially ready to appeal to the farmers in this House and out of it. But when a deputation of farmers calls upon this government, ' as they did the other day, to urge

upon them changes in the pork duties, pointing out that millions of pounds of pork come into Canada from the United States, interfering with the development of the pork trade of Canada, and asking, not that a tariff be a adopted equal to that of the United States, but only a duty of four cents per pound as aginst five cents per pound, the American tariff, we being six and a half million people against eighty-five million there, the hon. gentleman turns a deaf ear to them, unwilling to change our present duty of two cents per pound to four cents per pound, though the farmers of this country are so deeply interested in the question. I have no disposition to array the farmers against the manufacturers, for you cannot protect one without protecting the other. It is to the interest of the farmers of Canada, especially of those who are engaged in the production of small articles such as strawberries, potatoes, celery and many others that I could mention, to have a tariff equally as high as that of the United States in order to protect the farmers of this country against the surplus products that are sent in from time to time from the south.
It has often been said that under a tariff for the protection of manufactures, there would be combines to keep up prices and compel the consumer in Canada to pay these prices. I have no sympathy with combines; I believe that when manufacturers combine to raise prices the government should step in and, if necessary, take away their protection for the time being until they are ready to give proper prices to consumers But it is absolutely impossible to have a combine amongst the farmers-I think that statement will go without contradiction. If you have twenty manufacturing establishments turning out a given kind of goods, it is possible for them to get together and agree upon prices; but with millions of farmers producing the various kinds of farm products the government need not fear any combine in these articles. Therefore they can very safely give them a fair measure of protection so that the farmers, who are the taxpayers in the main, and at least as much interested in the development of Canada as any other class, should be treated on a par with other classes while there is protection in the country. I appeal particularly to my hon. friend the Finance Minister to revise his tariff. We pointed out to my hon. friend the necessity of doing this when we were enjoying buoyant revenue. I myself moved a resolution or two in the interests of our market gardens. I pointed out that it was in prosperous times that the government should alter the tariff in the best interests of our farming community. But my hon. friend was then too busy counting his dollars and to-day finds himself confronted with deficits. He has allowed the day of grace to go by. He has had $75,000,000 of 132
surpluses since his party came into power. That was the time to alter the tariff. That was the time when the farming interests could be better taken care of than now. We urged the Finance Minister from this side to take that course, but he turned a deaf ear to all our arguments, and we again find it our duty to point out to him that several industries, in which our farmers are particularly interested, such as wool; pork market gardening, require better protection; and I am one of those who believe that if better protection be given, the people will not be the losers. I do not think there is a farmer in all Canada who will say that the tariff in the United States should be double what it is in this country. Our people believe in British fair play and that is what we are asking for. There was a time when certain agricultural products, for instance barley, had a market in the United States, and our farmers benefited by that market. But when the McKinley tariff put the duty at 30 cents a bushel, some of our farmers thought they were ruined. However, our farmers continued to grow barley and also paid attention to other agricultural pursuits, and instead of sending our barley to the United States we consumed it on our own Canadian farms in the production of beef and in other industries in which our farmers are engaged.
The former member for Toronto (Mr. Brock) pointed out some years ago to the Finance Minister that if something were not done for the woollen industry, millions of capital would be lost. The reply from the other side and in the public press was that the reason why the woollen industry in Canada did not prosper was because its machinery was not up to date but antiquated and not to be compared with the machinery in the American and British establishments. Well, my hon. friend from Lanark (Mr. Thoburn) who is a practical man, engaged in the business, pointed out this afternoon that the machinery in our Canadian establishments is equal to that in the factories of Great Britain and the United States. That such is the case must be evident because the machinery to be found in the woollen industries of Canada is chiefly manufactured in England and the United States and not in Canada; and no one who is investing his capital in the woollen industry would use it to purchase antiquated machinery. Therefore we no longer hear that argument advanced. My hon. friend (Mr. Thoburn) also pointed out that the wages paid in our Canadian woollen industry were much larger than those paid in the British factories. Surely it is in the interests of our people that we should pay a liberal wage to those engaged in our manufacturing industries. That is in the interest of everybody. This allows our mechanics to pay better prices and consume larger quantities of farm products



and every other class of goods manufactured and grown in Canada. Therefore my hon. friend the Finance Minister, even at this late day, should see that some relief is given the woollen industry so that its raw products will be more profitable to our farmers and that the wages will be paid our own Canadian people, and we shall not import any class of goods which we can manufacture ourselves.
I do not want to repeat what has been so well said by my hon. friends who preceded me or to burden ' Hansard ' with figures, but I want to emphasize the fact that the government will not find it to their advantage to neglect the farmers any longer. Our farmers are now manufacturers themselves; and when the government try to draw a distinction between the interests of the farmers and those of the manufacturers, they will find that our farmers realize that in protecting the manufacturers we are protecting the agriculturists, that there must be no western or eastern Canada, that we must manufacture in Canada all we require, grow on Canadian farms what we consume, build up Canada by tariffs in a way that will enable our farmers to raise on their farms what we consume in Canada and furnish our manufacturers the opportunity of manufacturing everything we are capable of manufacturing within the limits of our own country, and thus pay wages to our own people and keep the money in our own country.

I desire to draw the attention of the House to a notice of motion which has been on the Order Paper for some time back, but which, owing to various circumstances, could not come up for consideration according to the rules of the House. This resolution, proposed by myself, to be seconded by Mr. Turcotte, the hon. member for Quebec county, is as follows:
That in the opinion of this House, so long as the Canadian tariff affords, incidentally or otherwise, a considerable degree of protection to manufacturers, some protection may fairly and properly be afforded by our tariff to Canadian agriculturists and stock raisers upon hogs, hog products, garden vegetables and such other items as it may appear possible to so protect with advantage to the agriculturist, and without undue injury to the Canadian consumer.
Whether we are free traders, revenue tariff men, or national policy protectionists would seem to matter little because the policy of Canada has been settled for the next four or five years upon a revenue tariff basis and it would appear to be our duty whether we entirely approve of this policy or not, one and all to join in and produce the best possible results for Canada and her people from that revenue tariff. And as our agricultural Mr. BLAIN.
interests are by far the greatest individual interests in Canada, it would only seem fair that the revenue tariff should be applied to preserve the home market for the home produce along agricultural lines, to equally as great an etxent as along manufacturing or any other lines, without asking for any special favours, but just equal consideration. Then if we are agreed upon that, the only reason I can see why we have not got it, is because as agriculturists we have not unitedly and forcefully asked for it, and without complaining or interfering with any other branch of industry, I may be permitted to illustrate the situation as it seems to me, along agricultural lines, as applied to the hog industry. During the years just previous to 1907, when times were good in the United States and still better in Canada, the United States surplus product interfered but slightly with us; as they had a fairly good homie market they were not so anxious to look around for places in which to realize on their surplus products. During that time the hog product on foot brought an average in Canada of about seven cents, which made hog raising a profitable branch of agriculture. The supply then was sufficient for Canada's requirements and we also had a very large surplus for export to Great Britain. When the financial panic occurred over the world generally and less seriously in Canada than in any other country, the United States holders^ packers and speculators generally looked about for a place in which to unload, with the result that with the very low tariff against their products entering Canada they were able to unload in this country at a considerably reduced or slaughtered price, but a price at which it paid the Canadian packer and speculator to buy from them. About that same time the filth scandals were exposed in Chicago and this created a distaste for United States products in Great Britain. The result was a further surplus of hog products in the United States. A rigid inspection was imposed upon all hog products being exported to Great Britain and millions of pounds were rejected, not altogether on account of disease but owing to the inferior quality, and this meat was slaughtered in both the United States and Canadian markets. This had the effect of bearing down the price in Canada to five cents or less on foot. It might reasonably be supposed that that condition would help the consumer to some extent, but we find tjiat since the price of hogs declined from seven cents to five cents on foot the price to the consumer went up at least two cents. Thus the tariff conditions seem to give the packer and speculator generally an opportunity to arrange his combine or agreement so that his knife could cut both ways; he was able

to reduce the price to the producer and increase the price to the consumer. That condition of affairs we do not think should exist and I do not think it would if we had a slightly higher tariff, say four cents a pound. The two cent tariff serves very well while times are good in the United States, when they are not seeking for a market, especially a dumping market, for their surplus products. But we know that in the United States they have a Wall Street in New York and a wheat pit in Chicago. We know that the Bulls, as they are called, control these markets largely for 25 days in the month on the average, but for the one remaining day in the month we find that the Bears get on top and they invariably force the price of pork down by two, three or four cents per pound with the result that Canadian packers, who have their agents there, buy sufficient supplies on these bear days to tide them over until the next bear day, so that it pays them to import and pay the two cent duty. If we had a tariff of four cents that would not be practicable or possible, and the benefit to Canada would be enormous.
It may be said, it will probably be said to-night, that the Canadian farmers and producers of hogs cannot furnish enough for the home requirements and the export trade, but as against that during the years 1904 and 1905, when we were exporting pork products to the extent of $12,000,000 to $15,000,000 annually to Great Britain, we were importing only about $500,000 worth of hog products. Since that time our imports have increased from half a million dollars, until in the last fiscal year ending March 31, 1908, we imported two million eight hundred and -some odd 'thousand, .almost Ithree million dollars' worth of hog products, and yet the Trade and Commerce returns show that our exports had decreased from nearly $15,000,000 down to almost $10,000,000. The Customs returns show that the imports are constantly increasing and that for the six months from June to December of last year we imported one million seven hundred and seventy thousand odd dollars' worth; if the same rate of increase continues to the end of the year, we will have imported this year about $3,500,000 worth. I estimate that to supply the Canadian market with the quantity of pork products of the various classes which we now im-[DOT] port, the product of about one million more hogs would be required. If we had one million more hogs supplied in Canada even at an increased cost it would not increase the price to the consumer a particle. To illustrate, three months ago the price of pork in Canada was five cents on foot. Today it is eight cents on foot, but I venture to say that the price has not increased a particle in any retail store, in fact I see by the price in the windows that it has 132i
rather decreased. If one million more hogs were slaughtered in Canada they would provide for the higher class cuts that are imported at the present time and in addition would provide a very large quantity of the cheaper cuts, not suitable for curing and exporting, which would require to be sold at home.
At the present time the packers have scarcely enough of these cheaper cuts from the animals that they have to slaughter to supply the home market, with the result that they are able to charge about what they like, or from two to three cents more than is charged in the United States. If a million more hogs were produced and slaughtered here they would have the cheaper cuts, not of inferior quality but the cheaper cuts not suitable for curing for export but to sell at home. That would create rather a surplus instead of a shortage in our home supply. We would find our packers, instead of having a combine to increase the price, rivalling each other to get rid of that class of product and they would thereby reduce the price to the consumer in* Canada. In fact the price to the consumer in Canada does not bear a fair proportion to the price the farmers are paid for his raw product. For the past couple of years, as far as my observation goes, considering the markets in Buffalo and Hamilton with reference to the freight rate to be about equi-distant, the price paid lias been half a cent on an average higher in Buffalo than in Hamilton. According to the price reports that the Department of Agriculture here have turned out we find that to have been the case to quite an extent. I hp-ve these figures here if my word is doubted.
Would the hon. gentleman say what his authority is for these figures?
My authority is the price section of the Department of Agriculture.
Of this government?

Of this government. That same price department shows that notwithstanding that a higher price is paid for the raw material there than here, the wholesale price to the dealer in the United States, is, on the average, about two cents less than in Canada and the price to the consumer about three cents less. That all goes to show that the Canadian packer, whether he cannot handle) the business as cheaply or not, requires for his purposes about two or three cents more than the United States packer. To my mind the Canadian packer is just as good a man as the United States packer and I believe he can do business just as satisfactorily, just

as well and just as profitably on the same margin between the cost and sale prices. I have no disposition to interfere seriously with or injure the packer in any way, but I do think he is taking out of the customer too large a share altogether in proportion to what he is giving to the producer, and I believe that the producer should have a more equitable share.
The higher the tariff the smaller the price.

It may be said and argued that the United States price and the Canadian tariff as between Canada and the United States would have no bearing upon the price of the hogs, or of the pork, because, as we export considerably more than we import, our export price, or the Liverpool, or British price generally would rule. But the same price reports that I referred to a moment ago will go to show that while the price to the wholesaler in Canada is two cents higher than it is to the United States wholesaler, the price in Liverpool is from two to three cents less. The conditions are to-day that if pork is packed in this vicinity, if the freight is paid from here to Montreal or Quebec, if the ocean freight is paid and it is put on the market at Liverpool, I can go to Liverpool, buy that same pork at the market price there, pay the freight back to Ottawa, open a store next door to that of the packer and if the present prices are maintained I can undersell that store and make a good business profit out of the transaction. That condition of things should not exist and if it continues to exist it is a pity that the farmer, the actual producer, should not get his fair share of that difference.
Our western friends will feel that an increase in the tariff might seriously interfere with them and affect the cost of their supplies. To my mind I do not think it would. Our western friends are to-day producing quite large quantities of pork, and I think it will only be a short time before they will be producing all they require in the west. In fact, I think they are doing so to-day, and that they will have pork to export before very long. Another reason why I think we are able to produce more than we require and have a considerable amount for export is this: During the years 1904 and 1905 and for some time previously we were struggling in the British market to make a reputation, and, by that reputation, get a more profitable price. The Danish pork in the British market is regarded as the best pork and it commands a higher price. It brings about four cents more than United States pork, and Irish pork ranges about the same. Previous to 1897 our Canadian poTk had improved in quality and in taste to the extent that we were Mr. SEALEY.
getting about three cents more than the United States product would bring. Since that time large quantities of United States pork have been imported into Canada, and as far as it can be traced considerable quantities of it passed on through and were exported in the hope and with the actual result at times of realizing the better price that Canadian pork demands of three cents per pound. They pay two cents duty on coming into Canada, pay the freight over, realize three cents and make an extra profit of one cent. That has continued for some time. The American corn-fed pork of an inferior quality has been going to the British market to such an extent that it has dulled the taste of the Britishers for the Canadian pork, so much so that we find to-day that Canadian pork has backed down to about the level of United States pork, and in some cases less. By the introduction of American pork here we have lost the splendid reputation we had built up and enjoyed for a number of years, and I think our western friends could afford to join in this movement to protect the enviable reputation which they enjoy at the present time. They are producing in the west large quantities of wheat-fed pork. That wheat-fed pork makes the sweetest hams and bacon, being equal to the pea-fed product with which we built up such a reputation, and perhaps surpassing it to some extent. Unless that reputation that they are building up in the west is safeguarded they will perhaps meet the same fate that we have met here in Ontario. Within the last year, as far as I can gather from the trade and commerce returns, while we imported of pork products nearly $3,000,000 worth we only exported about $5,000 worth. The average invoice price of imports of hams and bacons was about ten cents, while mess pork averaged seven and three-quarter cents, whereas the average market quotation is about two cents higher than that or a little more. The $5,000 worth shipped from Canada to the United States was entered at about seventeen cents a pound. As far as I have been able to trace these exports they are the exports of hams produced at Edmonton, recently of this wheat-fed brand, and I gather they have been sold at seventeen cents a pound; five cents duty has been paid upon them when shipped to Chicago, making the cost twenty-two cents a pound. One cent per pound for freight is twenty-three cents, and two cents for the merchant's profit is twenty-five cents. These hams aTe sold to people who can afford to pay twenty-five cents a pound in preference 'to American products, which they can buy at fifteen cents a pound. I take that as' evidence that the reputation of our western pork is well worth preserving, and when in a short time our friends from the west, produce all they require for

their own consumption then it may be safely said that they will not suffer by an increase of duty. If they can assist their Ontario friends without any detriment to themselves 1 am sure they will be only too glad to do so.
Do you say that your experience is that where the duty was increased the price of the commodity was increased.

We have had no experience of the increase of duty on pork, but I can say that the decrease in the price -n foot from 7 cents to 5 cents did not decrease the price to the consumer, but on the contrary the market returns show that price was increased during that period. Then, during the last three months when the price rose from 5 cents to 8 cents the cost of the article to the consumer has no been raised. Judging from this it would seem to be apparent that if we had a duty of 4 cents instead of 2 cents the price to the consumer would not be affected. I do not say it would apply to all articles in that way, but I do say that with the cheaper cuts that would be provided for our home market, if our packers slaughtered an extra million hogs a year, then, that class of meat being more than our home market would demand, a competition would be created that would decrease the price to the consumer. I may be wrong, but still I am firmly convinced that would be the result. The figures I have before me show that last year there were slaughtered 1,100,000 hogs (not including the returns from Montreal and some other places), and if an extra million were slaughtered it would about double the business of our packers. That being so, I am sure the consumer would probably get a cheaper article than he is getting to-day. There is no reason why the packers and producers should have any quarrel; indeed thev have not except that the producers feel that under present conditions the packer is able to so manipulate that he gets all the profit, and that when it is possible for him to do so he puts the price down to less than a fair living price for the producer. It may be argued by some that if this condition were brought about, agriculturists who buy lard, a by-product of the hog, might have to pay a couple of cents more per pound for it. I do not believe that would be so, but even if it were the average 200 pound hog produces about 15 pounds of lard, and if the farmer paid two cents more for his lard and bought all the lard in the hog it would cost him 30 cents additional, whereas, if he were selling the hog to the packer, as most farmers do. and got 2 cents a pound more for it he would be $4 ahead, and it would be a very
profitable transaction for him. I make a definite suggestion for the benefit of the powers that be in connection with the pork industry, and I ask for an increase of 2 cents a pound in the duty. I trust that in their wisdom they may see their way clear to make that increase. I have been much interested in the discussion on wool, and I notice that the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) who spoke as a farmer seemed to be more particularly anxious about getting the manufacturer an increase of duty of so much per yard on cloth and so much per pound on yarn. I failed to hear him make any direct statement as to what he would do about the duty on wool. Then, the hon. member (Mr. Thoburn) while he boasted as wishing to benefit the farmer, he thought the best way to benefit him was through the manufacturers getting considerably more protection on their products. He was looking after the manufacturers while he professed to be championing the interests of the farmers. The other gentlemen who spoke reasoned about the same way, but if they were interested in the farmers' side of the question one would expect them to be more definite. Our present tariff on wool is 2 cents for the preference, 2i cents for the intermediate, and 3 cents for the maximum, and I think the way to benefit the farmer would be to double that duty from 2 cents to 4, from 2i to 5, and from 3 to 6 cents. That is getting it right down to where it will benefit the farmer, and I have no fear that the manufacturer will look after himself. There is a definite proposition that will benefit the farmer.
Why don't you go higher?
If necessary for the welfare of the farmer do go higher.
We will take you into our party.

My friend here remarks that I will soon be fit for his party, but so far as I remember the national policy days, while the Conservatives talked about the farmer it was the manufacturer who got all the tariff favours.
The present tariff on pork was put on by the Liberal-Conservative party.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then why are you blaming us for it?

The Liberal party re-arranged the tariffs and reduced the customs duty on many of the necessaries used by the farmers, but all the same I do say that probably the Liberal government have not protected the farmers quite enough. I do not think that either of the political parties have given the farmers as much as they

should have had, and although our Liberal friends have done the better of the two I am anxious to see them go further still. The growing of vegetables is an industry which is of increasing importance, and I believe that without serious inconvenience to the consumer an increase of the tariff along some lines would benefit the producer. Take, for instance, strawberries, on which there is a specific duty of two cents a box. It is said that that is equivalent to 40 per cent when strawberries are five cents a box. Well, that would be a first-rate tariff at that price. But at that time there axe no strawberries coming in from outside, and it is the competition in our local production which brings the price down to that figure. When the tariff prevails, it is at a time when strawberries come in at anywhere from 25 cents to $1.00 a box. Two cents on strawberries at $1.00 a box is two per cent, at 50 cents a box it is four per cent, and at 25 cents a box it is eight per cent. If we can justify a tariff of 40 per cent when the consuming masses are buying berries, I do not see how we can justify two per cent, four per cent or eight per cent when imported strawberries are a luxury rather than a necessity; and if it is proper that our tariff should be imposed on luxuries, it does not seem to me that a better article could be found for the purpose than that particular article. It may be said that a 40 per cent or 25 per cent tariff on strawberries at the higher prices would prevent them coming in, and that we would get no revenue under it. With the small tax of two cents a box, there is not very much revenue; but a higher tariff would have one of two effects; it would either bring a greatly increased revenue, or it would reserve the appetites of the people who care for this luxury for the time when our Canadian berries come in, and when a duty of 40 per cent would afford a good profit for our growers, whereas they get no profit on berries at five cents a box. The same argument applies to cabbages, melons and other things. The duty on cabbages is thirty per cent, and at certain seasons of the year, when the early-ripening cabbages of the states to the south are produced in large quantities, they are brought into Canada. But we suffer seriously from imported cabbages when their crop is nearly finished and they ship them in by the carload at as low as $6 a ton, which, with the duty of thirty per cent, amounting to $1.80 added, makes a total cost of $7.80 a ton. The average cabbage weighs about five pounds, or 400 to the ton. That would be 400 for $8, or two cents each. The cabbages that are brought in at that season are generally of very inferior quality, but their importation has the effect of enabling the merchants to say: ' I can buy cabbages for that, and if the local Mr. SEALEY.
producers do not furnish a first-class article at as low a price, we will import cabbages from the States.' With a tariff of three cents per head on cabbages, I do not think the average consumer would pay any higher price, while the duty would ensure to the local producer his own market when the later cabbage comes in. I believe a rearrangement of the tariff in that respect would benefit the producer without injuring the consumer a particle. Another reason why I think the farmers should have some further consideration in the re-arrangement of the tariff is in connection with the recent French treaty. While I look for immense benefits to Canada as a whole from that treaty, one of the concessions made by Canada was in favour of French wines, which our grape producers, whether rightly or wrongly, feel has injured them seriously. They feel that in that respect their best interests have been sacrificed. Whether it will work out in that way or not, I am not quite clear, but that is the impression on their minds. These are some of the reasons why the agricultural interest should have more consideration in the arrangement of the tariff. I believe it would be thoroughly satisfactory to our manufacturers and our workingmen if they were occasionally perhaps compelled to pay slightly higher prices for agricultural products. To-day the average mechanic working in a city, without anything invested, if he has steady employment at the average wage going, which is pretty fair, is able to bring up and educate his family with greater ease than his country cousin is able to do. The special advantage of the agriculturalist is that he is independent and at all times is proof against starvation, which is not always the case in the city. But in a general way I am satisfied that our manufacturers and city consumers would welcome a better condition of things among our farmers. I believe I am voicing the views of the great majority of the agriculturalists of Canada and of a large number of the representatives of Canada in this House. As evidence of that I take the liberty of reading a resolution passed a year ago by the Swine Breeders' Association:
Whereas the pork producing industry is a very large and important one along agricultural lines in Canada at the present time, and we appreciate the efforts of the govern -ment in re-arranging the tariff so as to encourage its growth and improvement during the past, the results of which have been most satisfactory until recently, when we find that in the face of the present tariff large quantities of United States pork are coming into Canada, thereby reducing the Canadian price to producers of live hogs to such an extent, that under present conditions the industry does not offer a livelihood and in order that effort be made to remedy this condition of

things, it is hereby unanimously resolved that ne, the undersigned, members of the Swine Breeders' Association of Canada, request the Hon. Mr. Fisher, Minister of Agriculture, to cause immediate inquiry to be made as to the qualities of pork of various forms coming into Canada at present from the United States; also inquiry as to the tariff head under which it comes, as well as investigating the correctness of the price, weights, &c., as represented for tariff purposes and also that inquiry be made from those importing same as to the profitable business results of such transactions, and if after so doing all these matters prove correct and regular, then we can only conclude that at the present time Canada is being made the slaughter market for over production of the United States, and therefore the Anti-Dumping clause Tariff should apply or otherwise the tariff should be raised, for while we are all moderate tariff men, yet we believe that on any line the tariff should be fixed as to regulate the trade of so important an industry most favourable to encouraging home production, for with the present prices the packer receives in Britain as well as the present prices to the consumer in Canada the home producer should be receiving more than present prices per pound on foot.
While we hesitate to trouble your department in the matter we are prompted to do so by the alarming circumstances that there is 50 per cent less hogs produced to-day than there was -six months ago, entirely a-s a result of low prices and the unfair competition, whereas if properly encouraged the resources are quite capable of producing double the quantity of -six months ago instead of half.
In the above matter we feel conscious that being agriculturists ourselves and in close touch with the agriculturists generally that we are voicing the sentiment of every farmer in the whole Dominion or at least 95 per cent thereof, and if you deem it advisable definite assurance as to this would be forthcoming by petitions, signed by almost every farmer in the Dominion.
The packers can buy a stock of United States goods on a low market and tide themselves over until conditions are favourable to stocking up again. The fact of the United States being able to produce corn much cheaper than we can in Canada puts them in a position to trade on a par with us after paying the two cent duty.
While the matter is up, we deem it advisable to draw your attention to the splendid reputation Canadian pork has in Britain and to the importance of guarding this reputation and providing for the profits accruing therefrom coming directly to the Canadian producers and in that way avoiding the possibility of packers who own packing houses in both the United States and Canada as well, drifting a part of this profit to the United States by way of substituting the United States product for Canadian, made possible by the lack of thorough branding of the Canadian product, so the British consumer who is so anxious to support the made-in-Canada sentimental preference, as well as the actually better quality from being deceived by the substitution of the United States product.
In that connection the Minister of Agriculture did take considerable trouble and did cause a more rigid inspection to be made at the border and did improve the situation to quite an extent. The Minister of Customs also looked into his department and caused a more careful watch to be put on the entry price. When an article pays a specific duty, the average customs officer thinks it does not matter at what price it is entered; but if the dumping clause be applied, it is important that the entry price -should be closely scrutinized. That pork is bought and entered under value can be established by the fact that at certain ports, where the people are not on to the racket of the bear market in Chicago and Wall street, we find small quantities of mess pork, for instance, entered and invoiced at 10 cents or a little more, whereas we find that the average of the year at other ports is -down to seven and three-quarter cents per pound. The reason is that the price of some bear day is taken, and as any one can buy at that price on a bear day, the application of the dumping clause is not so easy to enforce. If it be difficult to enforce on that account, that is another reason for a little increase in the tariff which would counteract the practise of constantly buying on that bear day only and entering the pork at that low price. The Minister of Finance promised to take the matter into his serious consideration, but if the other two departments fail to bring about satisfactory results I hardly t-rmw whether we can expect -something from the hon. gentleman or not. However, representations have been made and the circumstances and conditions are known, and I do hope that the Minister of Finance will see that there is something in the budget speech for the agricultural interests, especially along the line of pork, vegetables and fruit, and others that could be improved and remedied without unduly injuring the consumer.
True, with rural delivery, 2 cent postage, &c., the government are doing well for the farm life comfort, but another step could be taken, by extending the same protection to farmers as to manufacturers, and in this way take one large step farther forward.
As to the packers, from the drift of my remarks it might be said that I am hostile to them, but I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I have nothing but the kindliest and best feelings for them, and if my views should prevail, I believe their business would double. And if they made a little more than half their present profit on double the business, they would still be ahead at the end of the year.
Is it not a fact that half the packing houses in the country are running at half time now?

Now, it may be said that the vegetable growing industry in Canada is small. Perhaps it is, when compared with our great agricultural interest, but it is a development of agriculture, and the more encouragement it receives the better field is left for general agriculture. But it is by no means so small as a hasty glance would lead one to believe. I am sorry I cannot, at the moment, quote the amount invested in vegetable growing, but it is equal to about half the investment in manufactures in Canada; it is something enormous, (Something wonderful; and in view of its great importance and of the number of people to be benefited without injury to the consumer, I trust the Minister of Finance will take it into his serious consideration, and that when the budget comes down we shall be able to welcome the benefit. While it is true that considerable increases of duties, as a general thing, may encourage combines, I am confident that, in this ease, the increases asked for would have exactly the opposite effect. While there has been some slight inquiry into the pork packer's combine, success has not been attained in actually securing a conviction, though success has gone to the extent of disorganizing their methods somewhat when the Crown Attorneys and other officers whose duty it is to follow this line have got after them. But it requires constant pursuit and constant vigilance to prevent their methods from playing greater havoc with the pork-producing industry than they do. I think we have clearly proven that this case of pork industry is one in which the theory of the export price governing the situation does not apply, for the facts show that, while, three months ago. the prices in Liverpool was slightly higher than here, when the price here went down the price went up in Liverpool.. In view of what I have said-that the agricultural interest must to some extent, bear the advantage given to the manufacturing interest and to the iron and steel industries, both by way of tariff and by way of bounty, and that the agricultural interest itself represents such a very large portion of our population-it does seem to me that it should receive thorough and careful consideration. In fact, I am satisfied that it is receiving that consideration. But it is results that we would like to have, and we would like them quick. I hope we shall get them the day after to-morrow when the hon. Minister of Finance brings down the Budget.

My only object for detaining the*House for a short time on this question is the important interest involved in it, and the important class primarily affected. I do not propose to touch on the pork ouestion. except incidentally, or to attemnt to follow the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Sealey) in his
argument, for he has covered ground which was not contemplated when this subject was introduced, the matter brought forward for discussion being the case of the woollen industry. But I cannot refrain from congratulating my hon. friend (Mr. Sealey) that, after the missionary work of twenty-eight years , in him we have succeeded in converting an extreme free trader into a thoroughly up-to-date, approved protectionist.
Only so far as agriculture is concerned.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sealey) is an example of the kind of protectionist we find on the other side of the House; they are invariably protectionists in matters affecting their own interest, but free traders in matters affecting the interests of others. But that is not consistent, it is not proper; it is not fair. The principle of protection must be right, or it must be wrong; if it is right it must apply all round, if it is wrong it must be discarded all round. If it is right it must be applied all around and if it is wrong it must be discarded all round-protection cannot be right as applied to the farmer and wrong as applied to the manufacturer. The principle is either right or wrong. We hold that it is a correct principle for the conditions in Canada and therefore we have agitated it and supported it.
I was glad to hear the hon. member (Mr. Sealey) discard a theory that we heard advanced many times in this House by the Hon. John Charlton. Mr. Charlton was the father of that argument which was presented to this House time after time as absolute evidence that protection on agricultural products could not raise the price that the farmer would receive for those products because we raised more than we consumed, and therefore had to export and that the price received for what was exported always regulated the price of the_ whole product. The hon. member says to-night that that is not so. I agree with him, and members on this side have said that over and over again. His friends have advanced that argument hundreds of times in and out of this House. The argument was fallacious, unsound, illogical, and I am glad to know that the hon. member at last realizes this. _	_
My sole reason for touching this question to-night is its great importance to the agricultural class. We are told that the agriculturists represent about 750,000 farmers in this country. If they represent that number directly they represent about five times that number indirectly; consequently they must represent over two millions and any question that affects 2,000,000 people must be important to Canada. It is an opportune time to deal with the wool and sheep question, which is of deep interest to the agriculturists. The Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) will make his budget speech

in a few days and what we are afraid of is that the many representations and appeals that have been made to him by protectionists as well as by free traders may not have convinced him that it is his duty to give better protection to the sheep raisers _ and manufacturers of woollen goods in Canada.
Last year wo Taised in Canada about 16,700,000 pounds of wool. That represents a very substantial return to the farmers of Canada. Washed wool last year averaged about 16 cents a pound, so it represented at least $1,000,000 to the farmers of Canada. We do not know the amount realized from sheep in addition to that but we do know that there are to-day over two and three-quarter million sheep in Canada, and if you value them at $5 a head they represent between $12,000,000 and $15,000,000. The farmer derived from this source last year $1,000,000 in wool and probably $2,000,000 in mutton.
The hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) presented clearly to the House the value of sheep raising to the farmer. First, sheep raising does not require a high degree of intelligence; second, sheep require little care; third, they are great foragers, and for nine months out of twelve provide their own food; fourth, they are valuable weed destroyers and every good farmer likes to have a number of them on his farm to destroy the noxious weed seeds; fifth,, they require but little care and will thrive where cattle cannot live; sixth, they are the best fertilizers of any animal, they fertilize the land thoroughly and evenly. For all these reasons, sheep raising is a highly valuable adjunct to farming.
We are asking that the government raise the duty upon woollen goods and do something for the manufacturers of wool. Why do we ask that? Because every year since this government came into power men engaged in that line of business have been failing. I wonder if the Minister of Finance has examined the list of woollen factories that have gone down in the last 12 years during which he has been in power and has been every year plied with arguments to induce him to assist these manufacturers. I have here a list prepared by the Hamilton ' Spectator ' some time ago from which I find that no less than 61 factories have gone down in 12 years. Over 3,500 operatives have thus been thrown out of employment. If every operative is the head of a family, and most of them are, this would represent at least 15,000 people who were dependent upon work in these establishments and who are in' a state of starvation to-day if they have not been able to turn their hands to some other line of money-making. The breadwinners on whom these people were dependent have been deprived of their means of livelihood and have been obliged to go into some other line of business. I would like to, draw attention to the fact-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Sealey) can only ask a ques-

tion with the leave of the hon. gentleman who has the floor.

He does not want to ask a question but to make a speech and 1 think it is rather out of time to break in now. I listened to the hon. gentleman saying a good deal that I did not agree with but I did not interrupt him. I am taking the list as it appears here and I assume it to be correct. As far as I know it is correct. I am taking it as it has been published to the world by the Manufacturers Association. What has thrown these three thousand operatives out of employment, what has injured these 61 towns and villages in Ontario, what has deprived the farmers of the country of the additional market for their produce to the extent of millions of pounds of what it would have been if these factories were in operation today? What has done all this? It is the special preference given to England on woollen goods by the present government. It is the refusal of the Finance Minister to come to the assistance of the farmers and woollen manufacturers of the country and put up the duty to such an extent as would save these industries that have gone down. They have gone down. Who is suffering? First the man who has his money in the machinery is suffering. The machinery is either sold for scrap iron or is rusting out. These spindles and these looms are not in operation. Then the operatives who were supporting their families have been thrown out of employment. The farmers have been deprived of the opportunity of feeding these people and of obtaining a better market price for everything that they produce on the farm and which was consumed by these industries or by those employed in them. It injures directly and indirectly, first the men who are supporting their families, second, those who have money invested in the machinery and, third, the farmers who are deprived of that additional market. Yet the government are absolutely indifferent to the wants of the people. Is it not about time that we should try, by some means or other, to make a stronger impression upon the Minister of Finance than has been made heretofore? He has been obdurate up to the present time. He is about to make his budget speech. He has told us over and over again that he cannot announce in advance what he is going to do with the tariff, whether he is going to raise it or lower it. We are trying to urge him to raise it and we are plying him with arguments why he should do so because we believe it important in the interest of the people that he should raise the tariff. Take the town of Hespeler alone; two mills have gone down there. They have been obliged to shut down. What was invested in these two mills. The people that were running these mills had invested $750,000 in them
and they were employing over 600 hands. Take 600 operatives out of any small town and see how it paralyses the place, see how it reduces the consumption. These families must move away Decause they are educated in that line, they will follow it and if they are denied the opportunity to labour at home many of them will go to the United States to secure work. It they are deprived of employment in Hespeler they will go somewhere else and if they go to Almonte and find the factories are closed there they will ultimately be driven to the country that gives them employment in this line. See what it means to that small town. This is one of the live towns of this country inhabited largely by Germans. What does it mean to have $750,000 worth of machinery thrown out of operation? There you have 600 hands out of employment and a consequent loss to the farmers who supply the wool to keep the factories going, and who supply the other products of their farm to feed the working people. In that one small town the farmers' market has been -reduced to the extent of at least what is necessary to supply 1,800 people. Take these 61 towns and look what it means in the aggregate to the province of Ontario. And yet, although the woollen mill owners and the farmers have appealed to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs over and over again and told them that the industry was going to the wall, they remain obdurate. We make a last appeal to them to-night. I can tell the Minister of Finance that there was no more potent argument than this in favour of the Conservative policy in my last campaign, and night after night many reformers told me that they were surprised their friends were so indifferent to the interests of the farmers. We appeal to the government on this question for the last time to-night. We tell the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Customs that if they do not take action that industry will go to the wall as sure as the sun rises and sets, and the time will come when many of the friends of the minister, protectionists as they are to-day, will be so disgusted with the policy of the government that they will vote against them in hundreds, and sooner or later the government will reap the reward of its ill-designed policy. Most of the farmers in my constituency raise sheep and I myself have experience in that branch of agriculture. A few years ago I sold out a flock of 150 sheep because they did not pay. Unwashed wool was running from seven to eight cents, and washed wool from 14 to 16 cents per lb. Last year washed wool was 26 cents or 27 cents but we may take it at an average of 15 cents for many years, and while lambs are worth $5 each when they

weigh over 40 pounds in the spring of the year, in the fall they are only worth $3, and sheep raising does not pay at these prices. Why is wool so cheap? It is because we are importing 6,000,000 pounds annually and killing off the factories that use the long Canadian wool. There	are	not	nearly, as many sheep in Canada now as there were years	ago,	and	the	numberwill be getting	fewer	in	the	future.The shoddy imported goods are taking the place of the solid woollen goods which were formerly made out of Canadian wool. You	can	buy	cheap horse
blankets all over the country, and although they appear all right they are simply made out of shoddy, and in a few months they fall to pieces. So long as they are cheap they will be bought.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Once only; my hon. friend will not do it again.

I bought them once and only once, but I have seen them all over the country. It seems to be human nature, especially when money is not plentiful, to buy a cheap article although in the end it may not be as good value as the more expensive kind. As long as you give that British preference as it is to-day, and allow these shoddy goods to come in, so long will the woollen manufacturers of this country suffer and the farmers suffer with them. Last year we imported $22,894,000 worth of wool and woollen goods, and there is not the slightest doubt whatever that under paternal protection three-fourths or four-fifths of the woollen goods would be made at home, giving employment to labour and giving better markets and better returns to the farmer. Sound economic principles require that each should work for the other; we are not living for ourselves; the artisan in the woollen factory works for me as I work for him, and the wise policy is that the people of a country should work within themselves to produce everything within the country that it is possible to produce. It is because we are not doing that in Canada that I appeal to the government to-night. If we pursue that policy we will be doing what is best for the farmers, and for the settlers who will get into our illimitable western regions to raise sheep by the millions; we will be doing good to the manufacturer and to the artisan who must support his family from the product of his labour. If we pursue that policy we will be helping along the progress of our country. I trust the scales have at last fallen from the eyes of the Minister of Finance and that he has come to the conclusion at last that he should be a protectionist.

My colleague the Minister of Finance has never shown indiffer-Mr. SPROULE.
ence to any of the deputations that waited upon him, nor has he been indifferent to the remarks of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sproule) and others who have spoken tonight. But if they are really desirous of haying a duty on wool would he have any objection to state what that duty should be?

Personally I cannot say because it is a question that would require to be figured out very accurately by experts. We do not know that all who are regarded as experts say that this duty is necessary. It is not for us to say how much or how little the duty shall be raised.
The hon. gentleman says that wool is selling at 16 cents when it should sell at 25 cents or 26 cents, but the figures presented to us show that it is selling at a much lower figure.
Unwashed wool is selling at seven cents or eight cents.
Yes. Now, is it the idea of the hon. gentleman that in order to increase the price to the former figure there should be a duty of 10 cents a pound?
I do not know how much it would take.
The hon. gentleman is finding fault with us, and he should have thought that out.

I know that all this wool is supplied by some other country. If we were making all these woollen goods at home, our factories, instead of using about 12,000,000 pounds of wool, as they are doing to-day, would be using between 30,000,000 and 40,000,000 pounds, and the result would be that our farmers would get a little better price for their wool and what is coming in would be kept out.

The American tariff imposes a duty of 10 or 12 cents a pound on wool. I would like to ask the hon. member for North Lanark: supposing 10 cents a pound were put upon wool by our tariff, what would have to be the tariff on manufactured woollen cloths which now bear 30 per cent?

It would require some little figuring to say exactly what the corresponding duty should be; but if the duty on wool going into the United States is ten cents a pound, then, as far as I can see, we would want the same duty on the manufactured article that is imposed on the manufactured article going into the United States, whatever that duty is.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: That is 100 per cent in some instances.

If you put the same duty on wool that the United States puts

on, why should we not have the same duty on the manufactured article? I am not advocating that, but I am asking that question.

I only want it to be known to the people of the country what duty must be put on wool to protect the farmers, according to the ideas of hon. gentlemen opposite, and what duty must be put upon woollen cloths. If the people of the country will have to pay 70 or 80 per cent on their woollen cloths, they ought to know it. Does the hon. gentleman think that the people of the country, the farmers and the workingmen, would ask for that?

The hon. gentleman forgets that it would be very easy to carry the ten cents a pound on the finished goods coming into the country. That has been done before, and that is the plan adopted in the United States in a number of cases.
But you want to reduce it to an ad valorem basis to see where you are.

The hon. gentleman is all ad valorem. He never thinks of putting on a specific duty. It is not necessary to reduce a specific duty to an ad valorem basis. If it is a specific in the one case, why should it not be in the other?
If you put a duty of ten cents a pound on wool, would not the cheaper quality of woollen goods be taxed higher than the other?
The hon. gentleman's question answers itself.

Has the Minister of Customs forgotten all the statements put before him and the other members of the government by the various parties interested, dealing with the very questions which he is now discussing ? For instance, the Sheep Breeders' Association came here and represented what duty they wanted on wool ; and the manufacturers have been here time and again representing what they thought ought to be done. Has the Minister of Customs forgotten completely what these gentlemen have been representing to him ?
No, I have not forgotten.
Then I do not think the hon. minister needs information.
The manufacturers did not propose any duty on wool.
They proposed a duty on what they were interested in, and the sheep breeders proposed a duty on wool when they waited on the minister.
I had an interview with the sheep breeders within a week, I think.
I must call the attention of the Speaker to the fact that all this is irregular. There is a debate going on, and a number of members wish to speak.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The point of order is well taken, but it was the evident desire of the House to have these questions discussed, and I have not interfered.

As a matter of courtesy I may be allowed to reply to the hon. gentleman's question. I had an interview with the sheep breeders within a week, and their representation was that if there was a higher duty placed on woollen goods, there must be a duty placed on wool. I therefore ask the hon. member for North Lanark if the woollen manufacturers would not be in a worse position under such circumstances than they are now, with free wool and a reasonable duty on woollen goods?

If I may be perinitted to answer the hon. gentleman, I may say that I pointed out clearly that when the woollen industry of this country was in a flourishing condition, there was a much higher price paid for wool, with the duty as it is at the present time. If the hon. gentleman will take my advice and rearrange the tariff on woollen goods, I cannot see why that state of affairs should not come around again, from the natural demand that will be created by the increased manufacture of woollen goods in Canada, and the increased price of wool to the Canadian farmer. I pointed out that there was a time when we paid as much as 52 cents a pound for Canadian wool, with the duty just the same as it is now. Why were we able to do that? Simply because the mills were all in operation, using Canadian wool. But owing to the change in the tariff on the manufactured article, there has been such an importation of English woollen goods into this country that they have displaced the demand for Canadian wool, and consequently the price of Canadian wool decreased until it has reached the price at which it stands to-day. Just what corresponding duty would be required on the manufactured article if you put ten cents a pound on wool I am not prepared to say. I am not engaged in the manufacture of tweeds; I am engaged in the manufacture of flannels, and speak from that standpoint; but I would not like to speak for the general manufacturers of tweeds in the Dominion of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, as a farmer and a producer

of wool I would like to say a few words on this question. I notice that there is a tendency on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite to extol the position of the farmer as compared with that of other classes, and to call upon the government on every possible occasion to do something for him. That is all very fine if it were only genuine and honest, but the trouble is that whenever they call on the government to do something for the farmer we find a rider attached to their proposition, the effect of which is that for every $5 bill the farmer will get, which in the end is likely to prove worthless, he is asked to contribute $10 or $20 out of his own hard earned money.
In this proposition regarding the great woollen industry, there have been some statements made by hon. gentlemen opposite which I should like to correct. For instance, they have made several references to what the sheep breeders have asked from the government. Well, I am myself interested in the sheep industry, probably as much as any otheT man in the Dominion, and I am in a position to speak with a knowledge of the business at first hand. When a deputation of the sheep breeders waited on the government they submitted the proposition, as the Minister of Customs has. stated, that if any bounty or increase in the tariff were to be given the manufacturers, a corresponding bounty or increase should be given the producers of wool. But at the same time they pointed out that, in their opinion, it was a matter of very grave doubt whether any imposition of duty on wool would be of any benefit to the farmers of this country. In that connection I wish to express my most emphatic approval of the opinion that we cannot put a tariff on wool which is going to be of any benefit to our producers. If we follow up the argument of the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), who has said that a duty on foreign woollens would increase the manufacture of Canadian woollens and thereby benefit our farmers, we will find that that theory was exploded long ago. As the hon. member for Peel (Mr: Blain) has said, the Conservative government, during the eighteen years it was in power, took upon itself to teach the Canadian people what tariff protection was going to do, particularly for our farmers and incidentally for the people at large. But what was the result of their teaching? I sincerely trust we shall never have a repetition of that eighteen years rule which ended so disastrously to our farmers. It was the hon member for North Lanark (Mr. Tho-burn), I think, who said that the duty simply meant a trifling matter of 35 cents to 40 cents per suit of clothes which a farmer would have to pay extra to our Canadian manufacturers. Let me tell that hon. gentleman that at the end of that Mr. A. W. SMITH.
eighteen years it was a veTy small revenue which the manufacturers of woollen goods of any description got from the agricultural community, because it would take the accumulated savings of years to enable the farmer to be in a position to purchase that suit of clothes. When he only got 15 or 16 cents a bushel for his oats; when he had to draw his wheat to market and sell it at 45 to 50 cents; when a buyer could take the pick of his horses at any price he was willing to pay, and when he got correspondingly low prices for his cattle, and had to sell his lambs at $2 to $2.50 a piece, then was the time when he felt that the eighteen years of teaching along the line of protection had brought him nothing but disaster.
What has this government done to increase the prosperity of the farmer by the way of changing the tariff?

I shall endeavour to answer that question. When the present government appealed to the people to give them control and the opportunity to improve our condition, they promised to reduce the tariff where possible and in that way make it easier for our farmers to succeed in their business.
We never heard any of those statements.

My hon. friend must have been living very far back in the back woods if he did not hear them. I recollect quite well hearing them. In fact, I made the statement myself that such and such things would follow if the Liberals were allowed to take the reins of power. Well, some hon. gentlemen have spoken about a commission going to the people and asking what should be done. As soon as the present government came into office they took just such a course. I myself had the pri vilege of appearing before that commission on more than one occasion to represent the interests of the farmers, and the result was the tariff was removed entirely from quite a large number of products which the farmer required and lowered in the case of a great many others. A corresponding decrease in the duties on the raw products of the manufacture was made, the wheels of commerce were set in motion again, and prosperity came back to the farm. As an actual result we have had for several years great prosperity among our farming community. They do not expect to become millionaires, but they do claim the privilege of enjoying a good fair living and making probably a little more than they need for the actual wants of themselves and their families.	.
The hon. member for Peel (Mr. Blain) has suggested that after a very high tariff was put on woollens in the United States,

prosperity followed and that on the other hand, under the 25 or 30 per cent tariff in favour of woollens manufactured in Canada, our sheep industry has become practically paralysed. I wish to point out to the hon. gentleman that in the United States, with their very high tariff, there has been a corresponding decrease in the number of sheep. These things do not hang together very well. I desire to point out, further, that our sheep industry does not depend upon the price of wool. We produce sheep not for wool but for mutton products. These are more profitable than any other class of sheep we can raise on the farm; we can raise them more cheaply and they command a higher price. The hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) at great length dealt with the advisability of sheep raising and how profitable it was, and then he wound up by saying that we had discarded sheep because they were not profitable. That has not been the experience of the sheep raisers of this country. The sheep raisers have found, as I have said, that if they raise the proper class of sheep, the class demanded by the market, they can make the industry more profitable, and make larger gains out of it, and do it with less work.
If that be the fact, how does the hon. gentleman (Mr. A. W. Smith) account for the reduction in the number of sheep as compared with a few years ago?
I will try to answer that question also. One of the principal reasons for the reduction in the number of sheep in this country is the lack of protection from dogs.
Dogs with two legs?

No, dogs with four legs. Efforts have been made by the farmers for many years, through their associations, to induce the provincial government to put a law upon the statute-book of Ontario-and I believe the same has been sought in other provinces-that will protect the sheep from the ravages of dogs. When dogs get into a flock of sheep, though they may kill only four or five out of the whole flock of perhaps a hundred, the loss is not so much in those that are killed as in the loss of flesh and loss of constitution caused by sheep being overheated and over excited by the worrying of the dogs. There is another reason for the reduction of the number of sheep in the older provinces, and that is that it is found that better fencing is necessary in order to keep sheep. When the farmers were allowed to pasture their sheep on the roads there was less necessity for fencing their farms. In the old days, when there were plenty of rails, the farmer could keep his sheep wherever he liked, because a rail fence is sheep proof, but the ordinary wire fence is not sufficient to keep sheep, and consequently it is necessary to put up
more expensive fencing or go out of the sheep business, and many farmers prefer to go out of the business. These are two of the principal reasons why the number of sheep has decreased in this country.
Now, I do not wish to speak at length, but simply to say, from the farmer's standpoint, that we do not want more protection given to the woollen industry. With duties of practically 30 per cent-for, I understand that the preferential tariff does not apply to all the goods imported-and with practically free wool (only $6 was collected in duties last year)-if the manufacturers are not in a position to stand with this rate of protection, the only conclusion we can come to, I think, is that our country is not suitable for this business. But we know that the manufacturers that make the best class of goods from wool the produce of this country are doing well. A great proportion of the wool produced in this country gqes to the United States, and is used in the mills there for the production of this class of goods, worsteds. If the woollen mills of this country would use the wool that we produce, they would be in the same position as the woollen mills in the United States.
How is it then so many of them break down?

Because they are trying to make goods that they cannot make at a profit. If they would manufacture the worsted goods for which they could find a market, and in which they could compete with other countries, they could keep their mills running. The hon. member for North Lanark (Mr. Thoburn) spoke of the difference in the value of labour in Canada and in Great Britain. I think he represented the matteT very fairly when he said that one good Canadian was capable of producing more valuable results of labour than the three he saw engaged in certain work in Great Britain. The hon. gentleman told us of seeing in Great Britain a man and two boys running a plough, doing work which one good Canadian boy of seventeen years old would do. I am happy to say that a Canadian boy, in the country at least, is a man for ali practical purposes. While wages here may be higher, the Canadian labourer, whether he be engaged in running machinery or in other labour is capable of producing a greater result than the labourer in the old country, about in the proportion that the hon. gentleman stated. In the illustration the hon. gentleman used, the work done was ploughing. I would like the hon. gentleman to understand that this is the machinery on the farm; he is working machinery, and is able to handle these three horses-or four, or even a larger number if necessary as is frequently done in the west-one boy would use that machinery quite as well as three or four in England.
