The same thing, I believe, will apply in the woollen manufacture as on the farm. One good Canadian will be as good as the three who are employed over there. Therefore we do not stand in as bad a position proportionately as the hon. gentleman would represent.
I would like further to correct the statement of the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) that the committee appointed by the Dominion Sheepbreeders' Association to meet with a committee appointed by the Manufacturers' Association to endeavour to come to some amicable arrangement by which they could meet the government on common ground, had reported and that their report was as he read. That committee have not reported at all. They were appointed to report to the Executive Committee of the Sheepbreeders' Association. I chance to be one of the Executive Committee-

I read from a report that was communicated to an English papeT on February 11 of a meeting that had taken place two days before in Toronto, at which a committee was appointed to confer with the Manufacturers' Association, but I did not carry it further as I had no information on that point.

That committee have not reported. They have endeavoured to meet the manufacturers on a common ground, but have absolutely failed to get anywhere near them. ^ The resolution mentioned by my hon. friend as having been passed by the Sheepbreeders' Association was offered to the association by Mr. Big-gar, the editor of 'Textile Fabrics,' but it was not passed or endorsed by the meeting except that because of that resolution as representing the views of the manufacturers the Sheepbreeders' Association appointed a committee to meet a committee from the woollen manufacturers to see if they could not come to some arrangement: the resolution was not adopted by the Sheepbreeders' Association.
The hon. gentleman from South Simcoe gave the number of farmers in porportion to other occupations in Canada and then proceeded to speak of the great benefit that was to come to these farmers through the imposition of a higher duty on wool. It would be very difficult indeed to persuade the farmers of Canada that it was to be such a benefit to them and I would suggest to the members of the opposition that if they wish to become popular with or to be endorsed by the farmers when they appeal to them for election, they must drop very largely the idea that they can make the farmers believe that by giving them one dollar and taking five from them they will make the farmers wealthy.
We do not need to drop that idea, we never had it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: You do not put it in that plain form.

That proposition is involved in the speeches made to-night by the hon. gentlemen. You cannot possibly benefit the manufacturer if you keep the duty on the raw material the same as that on the manufactured goods; you must give him a sufficient additional duty to make up the disadvantage under which he says he is working and give him a profit or the change will be of no benefit to him. I believe that the woollen products manufactured in Canada last year were worth some $6,000,000 and there was collected in duty on woollen goods coming into this country about $7,000,000. It would surely not be fair for the sake of that $6,000,000 of manufactured goods to ask that the $7,000,000, already $1,000,000 greater than the annual product of our woollen mills, should be increased and that we should be asked to pay $8,000,000 or $9,000,000 or possibly $10,000,000 in duty. That would be absolutely unfair to the farmers of this country and they would not accept such a proposition. The farmers of Canada are thoroughly conversant with the affairs of this country, and when any one endeavours to make them believe that black is white that person is going to be very much left; they will not accept that statement from the opposition in any case.
Did I understand the hon. gentleman to say that you could not convince the farmer that the duty was going to help him?
Yes.

Then how does the hon. member account for the fact that when the duty on pork was raised, within two years the importations were reduced from $21,000,000 to between $7,000,000 and $8,000,000? Did that convince the fanner that it did him any good or not?? If it did the farmers no good, does the hon. gentleman .think the present government were right in continuing that same rate of duty up to the present time?

The only benefit that it could have conferred upon the farmer was to increase the selling value of what he produced. As a matter of fact six months after that duty was put on the price of live pork actually dropped to a lower figure than it was before that duty was put cn.
Was it not rather due to the fact that it increased the market at home to the extent of about 15,000,000 pounds for his product?
No, it could not have done that at all. The export price in the old country is the one that governs the price of our pork here.
If he sold a million pounds of pork and had two cents a pound on that and if after the imposition of the duty he sold 10,000,000 pounds he would not have ten times as much?
As a matter of fact the production of pork did not increase by 10,000,000 pounds.
Yes it did.
No, we just exported that much less.
There is where it actually came in. It did increase.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention at this late hour to make any lengthened remarks on what seems to me to be a very intricate question. We have listened this afternoon to what was, to my mind, one of the most valuable speeches that I ever heard delivered in this House on a practical question. I refer to the speech delivered by the hon. member for North Lanark (Mr. Thoburn). I have listened to a great many speeches in this House, but I have never listened to one, from a practical standpoint, that conveyed the idea better than the speech of the hon. gentleman and I want to congratulate him upon his deliverance. There are other hon. gentlemen here whom I would like to congratulate, my hon. friend and neighbour from Wentworth (Mr. Sealey) has certainly made a most astounding turn. I remember, a few years ago, going over to the county of Wentworth when that hon. gentleman was a candidate for parliamentary honours in opposition to Mr. E. D. Smith. I remember well spending some days in the endeavour to educate his constituents along the lines of protection to the hog, fruit and vegetable industries. I am glad to think that some of my remarks have come to have weight with the hon. gentleman. He comes out to-night practically as a full grown protectionist with reference to agricultural products, fruits and vegetables. He has only to go one step farther until he will be duly qualified to vote with us on this side of the House. I am sure we congratulate him for the progress he has made. I am sorry I cannot say so much about my hon. friend from Strathcona (Mr. McIntyre). He seems to be groping in the dark yet; in fact, he is very far in the dark. He had the impression that practically nothing but free trade would suit the country. He does not see any use in tariffs. He does not know any reason why there should be such a thing. He has a great deal to learn yet along the line of legislation. But I hope if he only pursues the study he will become a follower of my hon. friend from Wentworth. The hon. gentleman who sat 133
down a few moments ago (Mr. A. W. Smith) certainly made some astounding statements. My memory may be short. I may have forgotten a great deal that occurred during the long eighteen years when that hon. gentleman and hjs friends were wandering about in opposition wondering when they were going to reach the goal of power. I may have forgotten a great deal but I confess that I was not aware that 16 cents per bushel for oats represented the value of that commodity during that time or during any particular period of that time. Would it be fair of me, in answer to the hon. gentleman, to say that on the 20th June, 1895, whilst the Liberal-Conservative party was in power, wheat, in the city of Toronto, sold at 20 cents a bushel higher than it did in the city of Liverpool? I might make that statement and make it truthfully. The market reports will verify what I have said, but for me to say that during the entire regime of the Conservative party that was the fact, would be an entirely different thing. I would not desire for one moment to convey any such idea. My recollection is that during these years we had fairly good prices for the products of the farm and I am sorry to hear the blue ruin speech that the hon. gentleman has delivered or to see the terrible picture he has painted. It makes me feel sorry to think that we were so poor during all those eighteen years. Yet I never realized it. I was in business during those eighteen years and business was always very fair I thought. We had nothing special to complain of.
Will the hon. gentleman allow me to ask him a question?
I have no objection but I do not wish to continue the debate for any length of time.
Will the hon. gentleman give an approximate idea of the value of farm lands in 1878 and in 1896?

I did not come prepared to give the approximate value of farm lands either in 1878 or in 1896, but I can tell the hon. gentleman that this country was mighty flat and the people were pretty much dissatisfied away back in 1878. They embraced the opportunity of making a change whenever the opportunity occurred and when they did make a change they held on to it. They never seemed to regret for eighteen years and they never did regret it along the line of the fiscal policy. We all know that the Conservative party were not driven out of power on account of their fiscal policy. It was something else that caused them to loose their hold on the government of the country. The hon. member for Middlesex made a very strange statement here to-



night. I understood him to tell the House how much the Liberal party had done in the way of placing raw material on the free list to assist the industries of the country. I confess I do not know what raw material they have placed on the free list.
Corn, binder twine and fence wire.

The most iniquitous kind of protection is, so the Liberals told us, a bounty. And to-day the government is compelling the farmers to put their hands into their pockets and hand over their money to the manufacturers of binder twine. Is the hon. gentleman who interrupted me proud of that? let him go and tell the farmer if he is. Short wool, raw cotton, and almost all raw materials that enter into manufactures have since 1878 been practically on the free list, and I do not know of any special article that the Liberal government has placed on the free list that would materially assist the industries of this country. The hon. gentleman from Middlesex (Mr. Smith) told us what the Liberal party had done to improve the condition of the people, but I wonder if he knows how much change in the tariff they did make. Let me tell the hon. gentleman just how much the tariff has been changed, in the words of the Finance Minister, who, speaking in the House, said:
It was of the utmost importance that we should maintain a strong financial position, and in view of the uncertainties as to the amount of revenue that might he produced by this lower rate of taxation it became necessary that we should take some steps to make good any possible loss that might result. It was thought that it might fairly be met by providing for the raising of some additional taxation in order to balance or make' good, the loss occasioned by the reduction of duties
it was^ necessary to have an increased revenue in certain directions when we were to lose revenue in other directions.
According to the Finance Minister the government were taking a little off here and putting on a little there, and I am not sure that they did not put on more than they took off. In the last revision the government was very particular to put a little more on than they did take off. The Conservatives left a duty on grey cottons of 22i and the Liberals increased it to 25, and white cottons which were at 25 were left at 25. But two years ago in regulating the preferential tariff they increased the preferential duty on the white cotton and reduced it on the gray, they being shrewd enough to know that there was more white than gray cotton imported into Canada, and so they increased the duty on the article of which there was a larger importation. so as to get a larger revenue. I want to say a word about the British preference, and I am glad to hear it spoken

of as a British preference, because I don't suppose it ever was intended to be a Canadian preference. I have always understood it was given exclusively for the benefit of the people of Great Britain. Some people think we get goods into Canada at a lower rate of duty, and we do, but the main question is do we get goods at a lower price. Do you think the manufacturer in Great Britain does business for the fun of it ?. If he knows he can send his goods into this country at a better price he is certainly going to exact it, and if you put coloured cotton at 35 per cent when it was formerly 30 per cent, and leave the British preference at 23 per cent, do you think the British manufacturer, knowing that we cannot import this cotton from any other country less than 35 per cent, is going to be foolish enough to send his goods into this country at a low price ? Not by any means. I visited the old country some years ago and I was astonished to see how they understood our tariff system. They appear to watch it morq closely than we ourselves do. They know exactly when to put on the price and when to take it oft. and for my part I can never conceive of a British manufacturer, knowing that we cannot import goods of the same class from any other country at a lower duty than 35 per cent, shipping his goods to this country at 23 per cent unless he exacted from the purchaser a very much higher price than he otherwise would.
How does that work with reference to woollens?

Do you mean woollen
goods?
Yes.	_
I intend to make special reference to woollen goods in the budget debate, and I think myself the time has come when a readjustment of the tariff on the woollen goods is required.
My question was: if the English manufacturer takes advantage of the preference to sell his cotton goods at a higher rate, will he not do the same thing with woollen goods?

I trust the hon. gentleman will not consider me discourteous if I do not answer to-night, because a reply might involve longer time than I have to speak. But I will deal with the question at no distant date, and I think myself there is a good answer to it. I cannot attempt to discuss the woollen industry side by side with the hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), who has made a special study of it. and the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thoburn), who has rare technical knowledge on the subject. He made a speech this afternoon which I think was a splendid speech. I heartily endorse what

he said. I have enough knowledge of mercantile business to appreciate fully the advantages which he contends would come from a change in the tariff on woollen goods. I have always regretted very much the change that was made at the time the British preference was introduced, because I felt that it was not in the interest of the people of Canada, though it may have been very materially in the interest of the old land. With regard to the reduction of duty on hog products, I can well remember the time when there was a duty of only one cent a pound on hogs coming from the United States. It was afterwards raised to two cents, but later that was reduced to one and a half cents. I was glad when the duty on hog products, such as lard, bacon and hams, was raised to two cents a pound. It has been a great boon to this country. Whatever has been the cause of the present depression, or whether an increase of duty would help it, I am not prepared to say, but I think we are importing too much of American hog products. Why should we import into Canada in one year 11,000,000 pounds of lard? Does not this country possess productive powers enough to produce that? We imported also 7,335,000 pounds of other hog products, such as bacon, hams, shoulders and sides. I think we should arrange our fiscal affairs so as to prevent the invasion of our market by that large quantity of hog products. Of pork in barrels we imported last year 9,204,247 pounds. Altogether our market was invaded last year by hog products to the extent of 23,325,695 pounds, according to the Trade and Navigation returns. Every pound of that ought to have been produced in this country. I do not mean to say that I would favour a tariff that would keep everything out. I am not one of those extreme protectionists by any means. I claim to be a moderate protectionist.
Not like the member for Peel (Mr. Blain).

I do not know that the member for Peel is so very extreme. I am sorry the Minister of Agriculture is not in his place. He went into my county during the recent election to speak at a great mass meeting. Four lines of railway coming into the county town, from the east, the west, the north and the south, were induced to give special rates in order to gather a large crowd to hear the Minister of Agriculture, and one of his grievous complaints against me was that I was a high protectionist. He told the farmers that I was willing to put a Chinese wall around the country. The Minister of Customs nods, but he would not say it just as the Minister of Agriculture said it. The Minister of Agriculture referred to a remark which I made here some years ago, 1334
but he was not fair enough to me to say that the remark was applied only to agricultural protection. My hon. friend from North Middlesex (Mr. A. W. Smith) warns me and others to be careful not to ask the farmers to support anything like even moderate protection; but I may tell him that this terrible assault upon me by the Minister of Agriculture, which you might have considered sufficient to have driven me from the House of Commons forever, only resulted in my majority being increased fifty per cent. I am not afraid in my county to talk about increased protection on hogs, on apples, on vegetables, on a variety of things. Our people appreciate that sort of thing. So strongly has that feeling got abroad in the county of Halton that it is actually overflowing into the county of Wentworth, and if my hon. friend the Minister of Customs is not careful we may soon capture that riding with our protectionist ideas, because the farmers there want to have the privilege of raising more hogs, more fruits more vegetables. I heartily endorse what the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Sealey) has said; I think he is wise in taking the line he has done, because it is the line along which I believe his constituents would want him to go. I hope and trust the minister will not turn a deaf ear to the appeal that hon. gentleman has made. There must be justification for it when a gentleman of the standing of my hon. friend feels it to be his duty to stand before this House, and, in the face of gentlemen with whom he has voted and associated, declare that he has broken away from their erroneous ideas and is now going to stand by the farmers of the country and demand increased protection for their hogs, fruit and vegetables. I have said before, and I repeat, that we are just as much justified in using the tariff of this country to prevent an invasion of our markets as we are in calling out the militia to defend the soil of the country. The greatest asset we have in this country is our home market, and we have a right to defend it by the tariff or in any other way. We find that out market was invaded last year by an importation of $20,962,753 worth of woollen goods. When our Canadian market was overloaded with that amount of woollen goods how can we expect our woollen industry to live? It seems to me that with such an invasion of manufactured goods, there is not much left for the man who is carrying on the industry in this country. Some of those goods paid a very high rate of duty; under the surtax over $1,000,000 paid 46 per cent. What do some of our low tariff friends on the other side of the House think of a 46 per cent duty on woollen goods? Why, that beats the Conservative party altogether. We never dreamt of such a thing.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Then my hon. friend thinks the duty is too high?
Most assuredly, I do.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I commend that to my hon. friend's colleagues.

I decidedly say so. I do not think 46 per cent is needed. Not at all. We paid dearly for that 46 per cent. It is put there, for what purpose? It was brought about by the preference. It is a part of the preference; it grew out of it. If we had never given the British preference we would never have had the surtax. I regret that surtax; I regret even to-day that there was occasion for it. Under the general tariff we imported $3,717,569 worth of woollen goods at an average duty of 34.41 per cent, very nearly 35 per cent, on these imports, and the average of woollen duties last year was 29-.10 per cent, 30 per cent, we all understand was the minimum preference; but under the preferential tariff, the duties imposed on all classes of woollen goods averaged 26-81 per cent. I make special reference to that because I think it was misstated by some hon. members who assumed that all kinds of woollen goods were paying a minimum of 30 per cent.
Having said so much and having congratulated my hon. friend from Wentworth (Mr. Sealey) on his change of heart, and having extended imy congratulations to my hon. friend from North Lanark (Mr. Thoburn)) on the admirable speech he delivered to-day, and the very valuable information he gave us concerning this woollen industry-having done that, I feel I should not prolong the debate further. If there are others desirous of saying something, I shall reserve any further remarks on the question until the budget comes down, when the hon. the Minister of Finance will probably give me the opportunity of saying a few worlds.

At this hour of the night I have no desire to take up the time of the House except to express briefly the public sentiment of that portion of the west I have the honour to represent. The question before the House is the one which has been raised ever since this parliament began, which will be raised from year to year until it closes, and no doubt will continue to be raised throughout every successive parliament. It is the old struggle of the privileged manufacturer against the consumer. My hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Sproule) said that in his own election contest this very question of an increase of duty on woollens was a prominent issue, discussed at every public meeting. Well, in the course of an election campaign there are many questions discussed and very few members who come Mr. HENDERSON.	'
to parliament can say that it was because of one particular issue they were sent here. But I can say that in the contest in which I took part this question of woollens was also discussed; and if there is any mandate given me by my constituents, it is to oppose any increase in the duties on woollen goods. We have had the standpoint of the manufacturer of these goods discussed, and also that of the wool grower. The people whom I represent use, perhaps to a greater extent than any other portion of Canada-because our people in that western country have no very great means and must use the coarser kinds of clothing-woollen goods on account of the rigour of our climate. I was specially interested in this matter because in my own constituency the statement was made by my Conservative opponent that it was the Conservative party which represented the low tariff idea in this country and that to return me as a supporter of this government was to return a supporter of a protective policy. I was therefore very glad to hear the statement of my hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain), who took the position that we should have a tariff high enough to keep out every dollar's worth of foreign goods which can be grown or manufactured in Canada. That is a good enough statement to convince my people that the policy of the Conservative party, of which he is a prominent member, is not a policy of low tariff but of very high protection. My hon. friend referred to the question of agricultural implements. That also was one very much discussed in my riding. In one of the first discussions that took place in my own town of Rosthern, at which the hon. the leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden) was present, with the member for Grenville (Mr. Reid) and the hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Lake), and where I was among the audience, I was rather amused to hear the hon. member for Qu'Appelle give credit to the Conservative party of having advocated a reduction in the duties on agricultural implements, and I was also amused at the attitude of the hon. the leader of the opposition who sat there and took the applause, which the speaker's words brought forth, as a tribute to himself and his party. I have never taken any other position before my people than I did, when the question came up, as it did in this House in committee, that I was not favourable to the resolution then submitted by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Schaff-ner). The House will recollect that the only discussion which took place at the time was in committee, so that there is no record of the vote on the division. But the opinions expressed at that time by the leader of the opposition and the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) were

certainly not favourable to the attitude of the hon. member for Souris. In my opinion, had the people of our western country been satisfied that the attitude taken on the question of duty on agricultural implements by the hon. member for Souris was that of any great political party in this country, which would become efiective law in the event of that party coming into power, the political results throughout the whole west would have been entirely different; and if it had been the Conservatives who, as a party, had taken that position, the province of Saskatchewan would not have sent only one member to support that party.
Did my hon. friend say he was opposed to the resolution of the hon. member for Souris?
Yes.
Then we do not differ on that subject?

I however would remark that our point of view and our reasons differ very much indeed. From my experience of the western people, I am satisfied that, as time goes on and our representation increases and as the policy of the Conservative party in the west becomes more advanced than at present along the lines of a revenue tariff-which was their position in the last election-never again will we have in this country an election fought by the Conservative party on an out and out protection programme.
It is almost amusing to me, having heard the statement of Conservative leaders in the west a3 to their attitude on the question of low tariff, to come here and find in this discussion a reversion to old positions, to find that the Conservatives in this House are asking that the duties, having special reference to woollen duties, should be increased, and declaring that the duties that we already pay are not sufficient, but that the manufacturers must be allowed to take more money from our people. In all these discussions, representations concerning prices are always rather discursive. If it were possible to bring about the results which hon. gentlemen opposite wish to bring about, to increase rates of duty without increasing the prices of the manufactured goods, I do not think that anybody would stand in their way. But I think it is a bad principle. There has been some discussion to-night with regard to the protection of the farmer. I must say that, if you have a bad principle in the way of a tariff for the protection of your manufacturers, it is just as well to carry out that principle and give protection to the farmers. But I always feel, as has already been expressed in this
debate that, though, as in the case of the wheat duty, you may tell the farmer that he is getting a similar benefit to the other fellow, and so prepare his mind for burdens which are very much greater than any burdens which he may think he is putting on anybody else to support him in his business, that I should certainly want to go very cautiously even in giving so-called protection to the farmer. In the portion of the country from which I come, there is a great deal of grain which does not grade very high, perhaps as a result of frost or some of these causes which arise in the fall of the year. One would think that there should be there a great production of pork. As a matter of fact, there is not. It is a commodity which is used very much in that part of the country, but I certainly would not propose in this House a duty on pork to get out farmers to go into that business. I think that what our people have to do is to get out of straight wheat farming. They have got to understand that they can make use of their grain by feeding it. But I would rather give them that kind of information than tell them that if they will only put a duty on some product coming from another country, they will be able to raise pork. I was told by a man in Winnipeg two or three years ago that the Christmas turkeys sold in Winnipeg nad been shipped in from Ontario. That seemed to me a very singular thing, a thing which should not be in a - grain-growing province like Manitoba, where fowl could be grown, perhaps, cheaper than anywhere else in Canada. But, if our western people want to go into fowl-raising, I think it would be a good thing if they did it to a certain extent, but I would not suggest a duty on chickens and turkeys that might come in from St. Paul. I do not think these things are brought about by tarifi duties so much as by farmers' institutes, experimental farms and that sort of thing. We on the prairies use a great deal of fruit. The argument is put forth here that farmers in one part of the country should be taxed to help farmers in another part of the country who are growing fruit. By doing that, you only increase the cost of living, and in our western country what we want to do ii to make the cost of living as light as I ossible, so that the standard of living may be as high as can be with the income which the farmer receives.
And I do not feel that this is a farmers' question alone. It is a question which affects our cities, towns and villages as much as it does the residents on the prairie. This matter was discussed in my own campaign, and in the city of Saskatoon and in all the towns and villages of the constitu-



eney, with one exception, the Liberal party got large majorities. I am satisfied that any proposition of higher duties on woollen goods would certainly not meet with any favour.
What about the province of Manitoba?

There is no accounting for the province of Manitoba at the present time. But I think that they will come to the view I have stated. Now, our people in !the west are Canadian people; they want to pay their share of taxes and they are doing it. What we want as far as possible is to avoid the protective features of the tariff. We want to eliminate as far as it can practically be done these features of the tariff which do not put anything into the public treasury, but which do put something into somebody's else's pocket. There is nobody putting anything into the pockets of our western farmers, and I am not advocating that anything should be done by which that result should be brought about. My hon. friend from Peel (Mr. Blain) suggested that because the east had put a lot into the railways of the west and had given a lot of land to the railways-I presume that was with special reference to the Canadian Pacific Railway-that that was a reason why we should put up with a protective tariff in favour of the eastern people.
No.
I do not wish to misquote my hon. friend.

What I said was that as the Canadian people had expended large amounts of money on transcontinental railways, therefore it was quite possible for one portion of the country to supply the other portion with any article of which they might be short at any special season.
That is hardly the point I had in view.

I do not propose at this late hour to make a speech, but owing to the great interest I have taken in this subject, especially the hog industry, the production of bacon and hams, I feel constrained to make a few remarks. Before the McKinley tariff was brought into operation we exported largely to the United States market, we produced a heavy class of hog, heavy bacon, hams, &e. When the McKinley tariff came into operation we were practically shut out of the United States market and consequently we were compelled to look to the English market for our output with the result that by careful attention to the requirements of that market, we were soon able to increase our exports from some $8,000,000 in 1897 to

some $15,000,000 in 1904. It was at once recognized by the farmers of Ontario, and I think of Quebec, that this was one of the best paying industries that the farmers had ever taken up. Until 1904 our exports continued to increase and everybody seemed to regard this as an industry that might be developed to an almost unlimited extent. You could hardly find a farmer who would not claim that the growth and production of pork was giving him perhaps a larger profit than any other branch of his farming operations. Since 1904 there has been a decline in our exports and during the last year or two the situation has become so serious that our Swinebreeders' Association have approached the government with a view to seeing if something could not be done to relieve the situation. Particularly during this year, we find that something must be done or else the pork packing industry in which we have so much capital invested, will be in a very critical position. We know that to-day they have not more than one-half enough hogs to keep them running full time. Several factories have closed down and a great deal of money has been lost, especially during the last year. The packers have paid fair prices to the farmers, more, I think, than the English market would warrant. During October, November and December I know that the price, while not as high as it is to-day, was still higher than the pork packers of this country could afford to pay and export their product to the English market. They were losing heavily on the product they sent to the English market during those months. The price of bacon in England was 42s. and 42s 6d, and at that price our packers could not afford to pay 6i or 6 cents a pound live weight. We know that as a consequence the packers have lost very heavily. We know that our own Canadian market has been fairly satisfactory for what we were able to sell here. I am not in favour of a high tariff for any of our commodities. I do not think that any industry should be bolstered up if it is not able to stand on a basis of a moderate tariff. Some would say, I suppose, that two cents per pound on pork is a good protection. I think it is on barrelled pork, a very fair protection and I am not in favour of an increased duty, so far as I understand the situation, on barrelled pork. Two cents a pound duty on pork that is worth 10 cents a pound is fairly good protection-and what is more we are not producing that kind of pork in Canada. Our trade has been cultivated and developed with a view to producing a lean, light type of hog, suitable especially for the highest class of bacon, and we have developed that trade to such an extent that I believe our packers are curing their bacon infinitely better than it is cured in the United States, equal to the Danish bacon, and I believe equal to the Irish bacon. I

do not believe that there is any better bacon produced in the world than is produced in Canada to-day. A duty of two cents a pound on bacon that is worth 15 cents a pound is not, I think, high protection; I do not think it is protection at all, it is only an incidental protection if it is any, it is only a revenue tax and a very low rate of duty. I do not think that four cents would be too high a duty on bacon. Some might say that it is protection. Possibly it is, but it is not a high protection, it is a very moderate protection.
Would the hon. member say that five cents was a high protection?
It is getting higher.
Four is getting higher than two.

I do not consider two cents a protection at all in the sense in which the word is usually used. Three cents might help to relieve the situation. But the point I want to impress on the House is that our farmers are producing a special high class bacon and yet our dealers are importing from the United States not nearly as good bacon and selling it in competition with our high class bacon to the extent of over $800,000 worth of bacon and hams and possibly a few shoulders in this past year. There is no reason in the world why we should not have our own Canadian market for this high class of bacon, and I believe that our own people will not object to this moderate increase, when they know they are getting Canadian bacon, the best bacon, better than they can get in the United States-and I do not believe it will cost them a cent more per pound if a duty is put on to protect this portion of our industry. If we could produce more hogs incidentally we would have more lard. I am not advocating an increase of duty on lard. If we could induce our farmers to raise more hogs and develop this high class trade and hold it for our own farmers and packers I think we would be doing a good service to this country. I do not think we could be considered as advocating high protection. When you take into consideration the quality and value of the article it is only a revenue tariff. I believe it would help very materially to solve the difficulty. The farmers would be induced to go more fully into the production of the hog that is specially required for the production of bacon. I believe the farmers of the western provinces could be induced to go more fully into this industry. We find that the government of Alberta have had a commission investigating this question and that they have reported to the government of that province advising them to build a plant to help to develop the industry. As soon as there is an assurance
that Alberta will produce a thousand hogs a week, say, they advise the government of Alberta to help promote this industry by building a plant and carrying it on in the interests of the farmers generally. Alberta should be one of the greatest hog producing provinces of the Dominion along with Saskatchewan and Manitoba. I believe they would be induced to give greater attention to this industry and I believe the farmers of Ontario, instead of raising less than they were five or six years ago, as they are to-day, would be induced to give more attention to it. I know this is one of the best paying industries in Ontario. Farmers are making money to-day out of this industry. We know that feed is high and that is one of the reasons why they have dropped out of it to some extent. We know that Danish pork is coming into competition with our pork in England and we know that in October, November and December, the price dronped to an abnormally low figure. Packers were losing money and they were not paying the farmers quite as much as the farmers thought they were entitled to receive considering the high price of feed. I believe it would help materially to solve the situation if a slight duty could be put on bacon and hams. I am not going to dwell at any further length on this question. I had thought of entering into some statistics but the ground has been pretty thoroughly covered. The present conditions of the trade and the quantities that are imported have been referred to and I am not going to weary the House by the quotation of figures along this line, but I would like to impress upon the House and the government that the industry to-day is not in a condition that is at all satisfactory to the packers or to the growers of pork. I believe that this incidental or very slight increase would help to a considerable extent to relieve the situation and I believe it might have the effect of stimulating the trade. It would give an impetus to the trade and it would not be amiss to make the experiment. We would not suffer from it. The advantages might not be commensurate with what we may expect to receive but nobody would suffer. We are producing plenty to supply our own home market. Our home consumers would not be compelled to pay a cent a pound more and they would at least have the advantage of having the best bacon on their breakfast table that it is possible to obtain either in Europe or in the United States.

(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, at this late hour of the night I do not wish to detain the House very long, but I have promised to my hon. friend from Wentworth (Mr. Sealey) that I would say a few words in support of his remarks. I think that the

time is well chosen, principally fox a member who represents an agricultural county, when a question like this pertaining to agricuture is being considered by this House, and the least he can say is to vindicate the rights of the farmers. It is important that the country should know how the people's representatives look after their interests in the House and after all that pertains to the farm.
We are confronted with the question of principles. We have been discussing tonight theoretically free trade and protection, and naturally both parties took up arms. I don't want to enter on this ground, but if I was obliged to do so I would take side with the Liberal party in favour of free trade, whose battles we have fought for so long a time. We all know the struggles of the Liberal party for the triumph of the free trade principles. These principles have been discussed before the people, and the people had approved them. I think that the constant development of the public wealth in Canada proves that it is in the true interest of the people not to resist to the utmost against the foreign industry because, in the long run, it is the poor people, the large class of consumers who pay the protective duty. These are the people who are paying the toll-gate of the customs. Being so, we believe that it is in the interest of the people that these duties should be the lowest possible. The true theory, the theory adopted by our party, is a revenue tariff, giving the means to administer decently public affairs, and I think we should not go beyond that.
I will, therefore, avoid using the words free trade and protection. I will confine myself to figures that will show a lamentable state of things. The * Yearly Book ' of last year shows us the difference there is between the exportations of Canadian pork to the United States and the importations of American pork into Canada. This is what I have noticed, and which seems to be very extraordinary. During the years 1904-5-6-7, that is five years, we have exported to the United States only 489,757 pounds of pork, which represents a sum of $64,912 during these five years, and we have imported during the same period 34,192,107 pounds, or for the sum of $2,521,436. In the last year, 1907, we have imported from the United States 7,500,848 pounds of pork, representing $615,000. We must remark that these figures cover only the nine months of the fiscal year 1906-7; when we have exported during the same period only 84,518 pounds of pork, representing $13,493. This is an enormous difference. These are facts which indicate that, for one reason or another, the pork which is eaten in Canada or put in tins or transformed into bacon and ham comes for the greatest part from the United States.

This is a subject of humiliation for our national pride, because we have in our country all what is necessary for the raising and fattening of these animals. How is it that the production of pork is so small in our country? This is a state of things which deserves the attention of the government. The proposed remedy might not be adequate. It is possible that if we raise the duties on pork from 2 to 4 cents a pound we would not protect the farmer sufficiently to increase his power of raising pork, but, nevertheless, it is a question worthy of consideration.
It might be the same for meat pork as it is for some manufactured products. We all know that when there is over-production in some line of goods, the manufacturers of the country combined themselves to dump in Canada a large part of this overproduction at low prices in order to create a disastrous competition to Canadian industries. We know also that measures have been taken by the government to' protect us against this way of killing our industries.
I have reason to believe with the hon. member for Wentworth that the same means have been adopted in this case, and that at certain times the over-pToduction in meat pork in the United States is sent to Can ada in the same condition; that is to say, in a way to make disastrous competition in our own industry. I think that the time has come to put a stop to this illegitimate and disastrous competition to our farmers. But most of the members of this House who are sent here to study the economical conditions of the country are not able, in a case like this, to discuss this question with the same knowledge of professional men. We have to guide us the resolution adopted by the Pork Raisers' Association of Canada and other associations of the same kind. These resolutions have been adopted after a thorough investigation of the grievances and a complete study of the remedies that could be applied. We have thus a congregation, a collectivity of farmers, of men of experience, who come and say to us: It is necessary to bring afloat this industry which is essential to the progress and to the wealth of Canada. We ask our legislators to give us the means to fight this disastrous competition from the States. It is proposed to Taise the duty from 2 to 4 cents per pound. It might be a good way; it might not. I know that the hon. members opposite will not say that it is bad, because it is in accord with their protectionist principles.
As for the Liberal party, I fully agree for my part with the hon. member who has spoken before me, that this is not really a question of protection. Protection, as we generally understand it, has for its object | to prevent competition in manufactured I goods and in arts. I do not think that we

can assimilate the pork industry to manufacture. There is no similitude, and consequently we cannot apply, when speaking of the products of the farm, the same reasoning as we do to the industry.
I think that the government, who has its eyes open upon all which might contribute to the development of the resources of the country, will note the remarks which have been offered to-day upon this question, principally upon the figures which have been brought to the attention of the House, and which show an abnormal state of things. If we import in one year from the states more meat pork and for a larger sum than we have exported during a period of five years, and we have there an economical phenomenon absolutely disastrous and humiliating for us. It is for the government to study this question, and I know that the ministers are able to take the necessary measures to have a stop put to this state of things.
I have received from the farmexs of the county of Quebec verbal representations and letters in which they point out to me the absolutely disastrous competition suffered by those who take up the hog industry. Those farmers supply some of the pork-packing establishments of the citly where laree quantities of pork are used for the production of hams and bacon. Now the manufacturers, the dealers of that city cannot successfully compete with the products from the other parts of the country, and even from abroad, because they cannot obtain the necessary Taw material under such conditions as to permit of their carrying on their industry on a paying basis. But I may be told, and this is the capital argument advanced by our opponents : ' Why, if your Quebec friends cannot produce raw material as cheaply as the similar product coming from abroad, and you have no right to complain, the less so as the consumer will no doubt ultimately pay less for his food.' Quite true, but matters have to be considered from a different standpoint. As I just stated, that meat being imported from abroad does not enter here in the most normal conditions; it is the surplus which is fraudulently -dumped into the country. It is not the regular trade, as those who aTe conversant with the matter know perfectly well.
At any rate, as matters stand nowadays, seeing that tariffs are being readjusted all the world over, the United States protecting itself against Canada, and as commercial treaties are negotiated between two or three countries in order to protect themselves against foreign competition, I say that in commercial matters, as on every other question of vital importance for a nation, there is no cast-iron rule or theory that can be applied. Principles have to be more or less mitigated.
Now, I say that if ever there was an occasion upon which the rulers of a country or those who are at the helm were bound to mitigate those principles it is at a time when we are called upon to deal with the interests of the farming community in this country, which will be one of the great factors in making of this Canada of ours one of the leading nations of the twentieth century. Such are some of the grounds upon which I hope the government will take such steps as they may think proper for coming to the assistance of the farming community, for which service the country will owe the government a well-deserved debt of gratitude.

Mr. Speaker, at so late an hour my remarks will necessarily be brief. We have had this subject discussed to-day by the member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox), who posed as a farmer, and by the member for North Lanark (Mr. Thoburn), who said he spoke on behalf of the workingmen, and now I purpose saying a few words from the standpoint of one who is interested in a woollen mill. Judging from the pleasant frame of mind in which the hon. member (Mr. Lennox) spoke, I cannot imagine that he intended the House to take his remarks seriously, nor do I think the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thoburn) was serious in oil that he said. Up to a certain stage of his speech the hon. gentleman appeared to be solemn enough, but when he told us he was speaking on behalf of the workingman I could not help doubting. Then the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) could not have been serious because he held the government of the day responsible for certain woollen mills which were burnt twenty and thirty years ago.
Will the hon. gentleman mention any mill that was burnt 20 or 30 years ago?

I am told that the Ancaster mill was burnt 30 years ago and that the Flamboro mill was burnt 20 years ago. Now, before I proceed further, I do not wish the House to misunderstand my position on this question. I do not wish it to be supposed that I am a free trader, because I believe that we should keep the trade of this Canada of outs for the benefit of the Canadian people. But, Sir, I do not believe in building up a high protection wall for the benefit of any one class. While I cannot boast of the long experience my hon. friend (Mr. Thoburn) has had in the woollen mill business, yet I can say that I have had moTe experience in it than the hon. gentleman from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox). In the town of Renfrew for 40 years there was a woollen mill, and three years ago that mill came to grief. If I listened to the speeches of the Conservatives in the recent

campaign I would be led to believe that that mill came to grief through the tariff policy of the present government. But that is not so. Three years ago the people who were running that mill failed by reason of bad management, and we reorganized the company, and I want to tell the House that never in the history of that business has it been so prosperous as during the last three years. I want to tell the hon. member (Mr. Lennox) that last year the net profit on that business was 29 per cent; the preceding year it was 26 per cent, and the first year we ran the business the net profit was 21 per cent. I wish to say one word in reply to a statement made by the hon. member for Lanark. He told us that the charge had been made that because of inferior machinery the woollen millmen of this country are unable to compete with the foreign market. Let me tell my hon. friend that to a large extent that statement is true. A few weeks ago I had the pleasure of visiting a large Montreal woollen mill with a view of buying some of the idle machinery, and I remarked to the former manager that it was a very sad thing to see the machinery standing idle, and he replied: That is due to the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government. He did not know then that I was a supporter of that government.

Has the hon. gentleman seen the published statemeent of that same gentleman in the public press, saying that it is by reason of the reduction of the preference that they were compelled to close their mill?

I care not a whit for the statement of that gentleman and before I am through I will convince my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) that it was the inability of these people to manufacture goods at a minimum cost that led to their misfortune.
I will show him where their equipment was absolutely unfit to enable them to manufacture goods at the lowest cost. Now, Sir,
I was in that mill a few weeks ago, as I have said, and I had with me a practical man, and when we left he said to me: 'How did these people ever expect to turn out goods at a low cost; see their dilapidated building and see their machinery in such a shape and so close together, that they could not produce cheaply.' I could not judge of that personally but that was the opinion the expert expressed to me. So I say, that is the best answer to the people who are making the charge that the tariff policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and his government is injuriously affecting the woollen industry of Canada. I speak from the few short years' experience I have had in the trade, I speak from the experience of that woollen mill that is closed down in Montreal to-day, and as one who is interested in Mr. LOW.
a woollen mill I say that the present tariff suits me.
Are we to understand from the hon. gentleman that the machinery in the woollen industrial establishments of Canada, speaking generally, is not up to date?
I am speaking of what I saw; I am not in a position to judge of the rest. I only speak whereof I know.

FIELDING (Minister of Finance) I hope the hon. gentlemen who have addressed the House this afternoon will not think it discourteous if I make no extended remarks in reply. They will of course quite understand that this is a subject in which the members of the government are all deeply interested, but still we are not free to express conclusions in advance of the budget speech. I do not think it would be desirable if I were to make comments on the remarks that have been made by some of the hon. gentlemen, even though I might think their arguments were not so strongly put as they themselves imagine. I can only say that the whole question has been considered in the past, is being considered, and will be considered by the government. That is all I feel at liberty to say at the present time.
Motion agreed to and the House went into Committee of Supply.
Some resolutions reported.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Before moving the adjournment permit me to say that two or three hon. gentlemen to-day requested information by way of return or otherwise before the budget speech would be taken up, and as I find I probably will not be able to bring down the information to-day or to-morrow I desire to say now that we will fix the delivery of the budget speech for Tuesday next and in the meantime the various returns will be completed.
I presume 'Hansard' will report what the minister has said so that hon. gentlemen who want the returns will be aware of the fact.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The object is that they may get the information before proceeding with the debate.
Mr. FIELDING moved the adjournment of the House.
May I ask what business will be taken up to-morrow?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We will take up first the motion that stands in the name of the hon. the Postmaster General, and after

that Supply, beginning with the Minister of the Interior.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 12.30 a.m. Wednesday.
Wednesday, April 14, 1909.
